Reading Decisions Before Spans: Efficient Generative Verification

GONG Yanbin Affiliation: ADIA Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    CHEN Lei Email: yanbingong@hkust-gz.edu.cn leichen@hkust-gz.edu.cn*Corresponding author Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Abstract

A developer checking an assistant’s report may need only an alarm that a claim is unsupported. A generative verifier, however, can continue decoding to quote and classify the errors. We study how much of that output is needed to recover its decision. In a frozen 2B span verifier, the choice between an empty error list and its first object precedes all localization. Native8 stops generation at this branch. The preceding seven syntax tokens are fixed, so Prefill1 supplies them as input and generates only the unrestricted branch token, using the same native instruction. On 2,015 code-agent TEST responses, Prefill1 reduces eager resident service by 84.84% relative to full generation, with released-reference F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41. It saves 31.98% over Native8 even though their logical token totals are identical. Under default compiled execution, the extra saving is 6.74–26.73% on the complete workload, with small decision changes. Controlled evidence interventions and first-location decoding establish what these shorter readouts retain and what requires further generation.

1 Introduction

Consider a coding assistant that reports “all tests passed” when its execution log records two failures (Figure 1). Before relying on the report, a developer needs to know that it conflicts with the log. A verifier can flag that conflict, or it can go further and quote each unsupported passage. Both outputs are useful, but they answer different requests: screening a report need not produce a complete error analysis.

This distinction matters for grounded generation beyond test reports. In RAGTruth, 43.1% of 17,790 responses across six models contain annotated hallucinations (Niu et al., 2024). Recent benchmarks cover code, developer-tool outputs, and structured documents, where span detectors generate error quotations and categories (Kovács et al., 2026). Compact detectors reduce verification cost by using cheaper models (Tang et al., 2024; Kovács and Recski, 2025; Belyi et al., 2025). Here we keep the verifier fixed and ask how much generation a caller must pay for to obtain its answer-level decision. Prompting that checkpoint to return a Boolean is one option, but changes the output contract under which it makes the decision.

The native format provides an earlier stopping point. The verifier studied here begins its response with a JSON error list. Before describing any error, it chooses between an empty list and the first error object. Opening that object already signals an alarm; subsequent quotations specify its location. On the development source, this choice follows the same seven syntax tokens in every output. The decision is therefore preceded by fixed formatting and followed by a description that an alarm-only request does not require.

We first stop ordinary greedy generation at the eight-token branch, a readout we call Native8. This removes error descriptions but still selects the seven known syntax tokens one at a time. Prefill1 instead supplies those tokens as assistant input, then generates one unrestricted continuation. The prefix chooses neither a class nor an error span, and both readouts retain the checkpoint, evidence, complete answer, and native instruction. Their input-plus-output token totals are identical. Their execution differs because generated tokens are selected serially (Leviathan et al., 2023), while known input can be processed together. The comparison with Native8 measures whether moving this fixed work into prompt processing yields a further saving (Figure 2).

On all 2,015 prospectively fixed code-agent TEST responses, Prefill1 reduces eager resident service from 446.41 to 67.67 seconds, or 84.84%, with released-reference response F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41 for full generation. The saving beyond Native8 is 31.98%. Repeating the complete workload with default compilation and CUDA Graph execution reduces this extra saving to 6.74–26.73%, at sequence limits eight and one. Corresponding F1 changes range from −0.12-0.12 to +0.27+0.27 points across the fixed runs. Thus the additional benefit survives both optimized configurations, although individual decisions and the size of the saving depend on execution.

Assistant prefilling and deterministic syntax skipping are established primitives (Hugging Face, 2026; Zheng et al., 2024). Our contribution is to identify the native alarm as a useful stopping target for a grounded verifier and measure the quality and cost of exposing it through these primitives. The experiments compare early stopping with prefilling under matched execution, test whether decisions follow controlled changes to the evidence, and measure the location information recovered by continuing generation. Optimized encoder and cascade controls place these readouts alongside cheaper model choices.

2 Native Alarm Readouts

2.1 The decision in a span report

Given evidence cc and a completed answer aa, we predict whether any answer span is unsupported according to the benchmark references. The original request is retained when it appears in the source prompt. For a verifier that returns a hallucinated_spans list H⁡(c,a)H(c,a), the native alarm is

y^raw=𝟏[|H(c,a)|>0].\hat{y}_{\mathrm{raw}}=\mathbf{1}[|H(c,a)|>0].

The first error object makes this list nonempty, regardless of which quotations or categories follow. All readouts receive the same source prompt/context, completed answer, and opaque identifier. Gold spans, categories, and generator metadata are used only by the evaluator.

Full generation gives two controls for this decision. Full raw reads list presence directly. Full official applies the public evaluator’s quotation-to-answer-offset mapping (KRLabsOrg, 2026b), which can reject a nonempty list if none of its quotations maps to a valid location. The controls share exactly the same generated output and cost. Their difference measures the effect of localization postprocessing, allowing us to compare an early alarm both with the model’s native list choice and with the reported official result.

2.2 Stopping and prefilling at the branch

On the exposed development source, ordinary generation begins with a fixed seven-token prefix ss. In this checkpoint, ss decodes to {"hallucinated_spans":; it ends before the list-opening choice. Native8 keeps the native prompt and greedy decoder, but caps the output at eight tokens. The parser checks the prefix and reads the branch without requiring a complete localization or complete JSON. An unexpected or absent branch is invalid and triggers no repair call or favorable fallback.

Prefill1 moves ss into the input by appending its seven IDs to the tokenized native assistant prompt. It then generates one greedy token zz over the unrestricted vocabulary. The parser decodes s∥zs\mathbin{\|}z, finds the first JSON object, and reads the hallucinated_spans list opening. The next non-whitespace character is ] for no alarm or { for an alarm; any other or missing branch is invalid. Only the syntax is supplied in advance. The prefix contains no class choice or candidate quotation, and the generated branch is neither masked nor forced (Figure 2).

The same parser processes Native8’s eight generated tokens. Both readouts return an alarm or invalid status and retain the actual input/output IDs. Appendix A specifies the pinned prefix IDs, decoding options, and validity checks. We selected the prefix on DEV; test outputs play no part in selecting a prefix, mask, or threshold. Section 5 compares this retained native format with a semantics-matched binary output contract at its fixed default operating point.

2.3 Why the execution cost can change

Let P⁡(L)P(L) be prompt processing through the first next-token logits and D⁡(L+i)D(L+i) a subsequent decode step. Ignoring bookkeeping, the two short readouts cost

C8​(L)\displaystyle C_{8}(L) ≃P⁡(L)+∑i=17D⁡(L+i),\displaystyle\simeq P(L)+\sum_{i=1}^{7}D(L+i), (1)
Cprefill1​(L)\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{prefill1}}(L) ≃P⁡(L+7).\displaystyle\simeq P(L+7). (2)

Native8 must select each output token before that token can enter the next decoding step. With Prefill1, all seven syntax positions are already known and can be processed with the prompt. The full evidence and answer remain in the input, and every supplied position still counts toward the logical token total. The possible saving comes from changing this execution order.

Prefilling is cheaper under this model when P⁡(L+7)−P⁡(L)<∑i=17D⁡(L+i)P(L+7)-P(L)<\sum_{i=1}^{7}D(L+i): the extra prompt work costs less than the decode steps it replaces. Batching can amortize those steps, so the inequality cannot be inferred from token counts. For long inputs, prompt processing can dominate both expressions. Removing seven decode steps then saves little of the total, even if those steps cost much more than processing seven additional input positions. We measure service under matched scheduling and repeat the comparison with compiled execution to determine how much of the saving remains after runtime optimization.

2.4 When the branch is preserved

If ordinary greedy generation emits ss, conditioning on that same ss yields the same next-token branch under identical causal computation, arithmetic, and tie-breaking. This is why Prefill1 supplies only the class-independent syntax and leaves the branch unrestricted. The identity concerns the native list choice. The official offset mapper acts later and can still suppress an alarm whose quotation does not map to the answer.

In practice, prefill/decode kernels and batch shapes can produce different finite-precision trajectories. Suppose the all-vocabulary logits at the complete prefix differ by at most ϵ\epsilon per coordinate. A top-token gap greater than 2​ϵ2\epsilon then preserves the winner, since its logit can fall by at most ϵ\epsilon while a competitor rises by at most ϵ\epsilon. Our traces store selected IDs rather than complete logit vectors, so they do not certify this margin condition. We check prefix and branch agreement empirically and report the resulting paired F1 differences. Appendix D proves the conditional identity and bounds the F1 changes caused by changed decisions.

3 Experimental Design

Full generation and optimized early stopping establish the cost baselines. Raw and official readers separate the native alarm from localization postprocessing; binary-contract and evidence-flip controls test its dependence on the interface and supplied facts. Encoder and cascade comparisons address model allocation, where quality differences can also reflect inherited detection capability.

3.1 Models and comparison points

The models are the public LettuceDetect Qwen3.5-2B span verifier and its same-training 307M mmBERT-base counterpart (Kovács et al., 2026; Marone et al., 2026). We compare full official/raw output, Native8, and the encoder at native and DEV-calibrated thresholds. For the encoder, an optimized FA3-window implementation retains the same checkpoint, BF16 parameters, FP32 rotary buffers, and fixed thresholds. This optimization reverses the earlier cross-model speed ordering, making the encoder the faster option. Full output is capped at 1,024 tokens, and all native decoder readouts use unrestricted greedy generation.

3.2 Evaluation populations and references

Development uses an already exposed Data2txt source from upstream TRAIN: 1,026 responses in 171 families. The main confirmation covers all 2,015 code-agent TEST responses, including 1,014 reference positives in 1,613 source-derived components. Methods, selection, and measurement are fixed before opening this source. Two further fixed sources contain 617 tool-output and 641 README responses; Prefill1 is not run on the earlier tool source. Quality, class, length, and outcome never determine whether a selected response is retained.

For a later comparison, eleven policies are fixed before opening a project-unseen modern validation cohort of 1,117 code-agent, tool-output, and README responses. Source-only closure links seven responses to previously evaluated inputs. We execute all of them, with the remaining 1,110 responses/639 components forming the predeclared primary population; the appendix also reports all 1,117 and each source separately. This is upstream validation, used to select the encoder checkpoint; the generator’s selection rule is unspecified. It extends the workload and cost comparison without replacing the principal TEST evidence.

The public benchmark contains localized edits and released span annotations (Kovács et al., 2026; KRLabsOrg, 2026a). Its code-agent TEST references include the data authors’ model-assisted triage and review. README instead uses lower-precision first-pass references, and some of its edits are detectable without context. Both models trained on unified TRAIN, so these experiments compare methods within the task against released references. Long contexts and realistic label noise affect hallucination-detector evaluation (Chen et al., 2026); we report each source’s provenance and complete selected population.

All native readouts receive the same evidence, answers, and instructions. The encoder accepts 8,192 tokens and the decoder 32,768; encoder truncation removes context only. The main analysis retains all 441 truncated code-agent contexts, accompanied by a prospectively fixed no-truncation subset of 1,574 responses. Source components join exact normalized questions/contexts and context near-duplicates with five-word Jaccard similarity ≥0.85\geq 0.85. These groups account for dependence in the summaries, although they do not establish repository independence. Appendix A records the full protocol and its revisions.

3.3 Quality and cost measurements

Positive-class response F1 is the primary quality metric. Paired 95% percentile intervals use 2,000 whole-component bootstrap resamples shared across contrasts, conditional on the fixed outputs and grouping. Before scoring against references, we audit the actual samplers, token IDs, offsets, and request counts. Native readouts and the grammar-complete binary control produce no invalid decisions. For other controls, invalid outputs remain in the record with sensitivity analyses; incomplete runs receive no partial-cohort score.

We measure cost at two service boundaries. The principal experiment uses a resident decoder on one H100 80GB in BF16/eager mode, without prefix caching and with at most eight active sequences. Original-order chunks of 32 balance the order of the three arms. Its resident service timer includes generation, parsing, and result handling; shared initialization and source preparation are excluded.

The later eleven-arm experiment uses one decoder sequence and a co-resident optimized encoder. Each arm pays for fresh service, including required tokenization, transfer, model calls, readout/routing, parsing, and the same minimal alarm write/fsync. Arms rotate per response. Shared initialization, qualification, probes, and full diagnostics are recorded separately. Figure 3 separates the experiments, whose totals cannot support cross-workload latency comparisons. Main-job GPU accounting includes startup, failures, and idle/CPU time, each counted once.

Relative savings use complete-cohort service totals, weighting requests by their measured cost. Averaging per-response speedups would give a different quantity. We also report workloads separately, since their context lengths, scheduling, and preparation requirements affect service totals.

4 Verification quality and service cost

4.1 Primary test: 84.84% less service

Across all 2,015 code-agent responses, full official, Native8, and Prefill1 obtain 83.4128, 83.6594, and 83.4304 F1, respectively, using 446.4075, 99.4773, and 67.6682 seconds of service. Stopping with Native8 removes 77.72% of full service. Prefill1 increases this reduction to 84.84%, saving a further 31.98% over the eight-token control (Figure 3, left).

Similar aggregate F1 values coexist with changes in individual decisions. Prefill1 produces 788/87/226/914 TP/FP/FN/TN, compared with 787/86/227/915 for full official. The token audit identifies two sources of disagreement. Although every full and eight-token output begins with the same seven syntax tokens, their first eight IDs differ on eight responses. Reconstructing the prefix before the prefill output likewise reveals eight differences from the eight-token outputs. The syntax is stable, but actual execution can still change the following decision.

The official reader introduces another difference when it maps generated quotations to answer offsets: it removes two positive full-output alarms retained by the raw reader. Interpreting the same generation with the raw reader gives 83.5363 F1. Comparing the two readers separates the native decision targeted by early readout from its later postprocessing. Table 1 gives paired quality differences and their uncertainty.

Full generation emits 95,134 tokens, compared with 16,120 for Native8 and 2,015 for Prefill1. Prefilling also supplies 14,105 additional input tokens, bringing both short arms to exactly 8,621,241 logical input-plus-output tokens. Their 31.98% service difference thus comes from execution despite equal token totals. Relative to full generation, logical token volume falls by only 0.91%. Token volume therefore cannot establish API-price or allocated-GPU savings from these service measurements.

4.2 Additional workloads and fresh preparation

On the separately frozen README source, all four decoder decisions agree on each of the 641 responses, yielding 98.5782 F1. Prefill1 takes 8.3065 seconds, compared with 85.2763 for full generation and 22.1382 for Native8, saving 90.26% and 62.48%, respectively. On the earlier 617-response tool source, full raw and Native8 also agree throughout at 90.9091 F1; Native8 reduces total worker time by 46.83%, with loading reported separately. These comparisons retain the source-specific references and timer boundaries described in Section 3.

Fresh preparation is included for every policy in the later 1,110-response comparison (Figure 3, right). Here Prefill1 obtains 94.4751 F1, compared with 94.4547 for full official and 94.5522 for Native8. It reduces service from 827.4728 to 47.4990 seconds relative to full generation, and from 210.7107 relative to Native8: savings of 94.26% and 77.46%. The paired service ratios are 0.057403 ([0.053997,0.061365][0.053997,0.061365]) and 0.225423 ([0.218730,0.234101][0.218730,0.234101]). Full raw and Native8 have the same aggregate F1; Table 1 gives the paired quality uncertainty.

This experiment uses a single active sequence and fresh preparation for each policy, whereas the original batch experiment has a different cost boundary. The larger savings should therefore be interpreted within this execution setting. Appendix C.2 reports all eleven policies, the three source populations, no-truncation analyses, and results for the full cohort.

4.3 Does the saving survive runtime optimization?

To test whether the advantage over Native8 persists with runtime optimization, we replay all 2,015 fixed inputs using default compilation and CUDA Graphs on one H100. The 63 original-order chunks each run both arms in AB/BA order, counterbalanced by chunk. Sequence limits are one/eight, with prefix caching disabled. Fresh service includes tokenization, generation, parsing, and a minimal result write.

Across both passes, Native8 and Prefill1 require 250.12/183.26 seconds at limit one and 166.31/155.11 at limit eight, saving 26.73%/6.74% at identical logical token totals. The saving is smaller at greater concurrency, and three of 126 paired batch-order observations at limit eight favor Native8. The arms also differ on 12/4,030 and 13/4,030 branches. Joining these outputs to existing references gives descriptive F1 changes of −0.12-0.12 in both limit-one passes and +0.27+0.27/+0.11+0.11 at limit eight; these differences rule out lossless decoding, and the reused references provide no independent quality confirmation. Initialization is timed separately. Appendix G reports every clock and quality result, with the earlier 24-input pilot retained in Appendix F.2.

Complete accounting.

The primary allocation uses 1,296 GPU-seconds for initialization, preparation, and decoder/encoder workers; the eleven-arm allocation uses 1,907. The earlier compiled-execution and binary-contract controls use 744 GPU-seconds, and the full-workload optimized run adds 1,697. We account for common work separately rather than assigning it selectively to one arm. Including all failed and exploratory allocations, total exploration uses 90,659 GPU-seconds across 121 terminal allocations. This total includes 747 seconds of auxiliary analysis outside the paper and is separate from the method service timings.

5 Evidence dependence and output requirements

5.1 Interface fidelity and evidence response

Changing the output contract to a binary JSON field leaves the verification definitions, categories, evidence, and answer unchanged. To make this control grammar-complete, its one-token mask admits all six vocabulary spellings of true/false with legal JSON whitespace, selected by grammar rather than labels. Across all 1,026 exposed DEV responses/171 source families, native Prefill1 obtains 94.36 F1 and this control 92.04, a difference of +2.32+2.32 points ([1.10,3.59][1.10,3.59]), at comparable fresh service (14.38/14.66 s). Both produce valid decisions throughout. The native precision/recall pair is 94.03/94.69%, versus 96.33/88.11% for binary: under these defaults, native readout trades precision for recall. Unrestricted binary generation produces 659 invalid outputs and is therefore not the strong baseline. Appendix F.1 preserves it alongside the earlier Yes/No recipe and incomplete-mask results. This fixed-default DEV comparison does not establish intrinsic quality superiority over score-aggregated or calibrated binary readouts.

A readout could agree with full generation while exploiting an answer-only or context-only shortcut. We test evidence dependence with 24 frozen tool-return families, crossing two recorded facts with two fixed literal answers to produce 96 inputs. Full official/raw, Native8, and Prefill1 solve all 24 quartets and all 48 fixed-answer evidence-flip pairs. A deterministic classifier using only the answer or only the context is bounded by 50% accuracy, since each answer and each fact appears under both label conditions. The models instead assign the correct opposite alarm to the same answer when the recorded fact changes. This control establishes conditionality for literal records; it does not test real execution success (Appendix E).

5.2 Restoring a first location costs more

Recovering a location requires continuing past the alarm. FirstQuote supplies the same syntax and generates until the marker that closes the first predicted quotation. The official mapper then returns an optional character location; an unmappable quotation still produces an alarm, without a location. Repair and additional calls are disallowed. The full control uses matched prefix/detokenization and, after completing generation, selects its first valid quotation.

On the already evaluated code-agent cohort, FirstQuote preserves every observed raw full alarm, at 83.5363 F1, while reducing matched service from 425.791 to 204.637 seconds (51.94%). It returns valid locations for fewer predicted alarms: coverage falls from 874/875 to 861/875, and offset-presence F1 drops by 0.5946 points ([−1.0496,−0.2048][-1.0496,-0.2048]). Recovering a pointer therefore gives an intermediate output between the alarm and complete spans, with its own service cost and localization losses. The appropriate stopping point depends on which of these outputs the application needs.

5.3 A fast encoder and selective escalation

The optimized encoder provides a cheaper model-level alternative to shortening the generator’s output. On primary code-agent TEST, its fixed-threshold F1 is 77.3345 against 83.4304 for Prefill1, a 6.0958-point difference ([4.0262,8.2156][4.0262,8.2156]). The difference remains 6.0398 points on the no-truncation subset and reflects inherited checkpoint capability, rather than a quality gain from prefilling. The encoder nevertheless has higher recall, 84.12% versus 77.71%. A fixed 18-source timing control with three repetitions shows that legal FA3 windows reduce its median service from 276.547 to 44.121 ms, reversing the earlier warm speed ordering. The generator readout offers higher F1 in this comparison, while the optimized encoder offers lower service cost.

A physical cascade combines these options by running the encoder on every response and escalating uncertain cases to Prefill1. Let mm be the maximum answer-token logit difference, with calibrated decision 𝟏[m>t]\mathbf{1}[m>t]. Centered routing escalates when |m−t|≤rq|m-t|\leq r_{q}; the simpler Abs0 control uses |m||m| and the same calibrated fallback. Five source-fold DEV estimates precede one all-DEV fit, fixing the threshold at −0.935546875-0.935546875. The DEV quantiles are q∈{.10,.25,.50}q\in\{.10,.25,.50\}, with .25.25 primary. Routes and thresholds remain fixed on modern validation. Equal-call hash routing measures the value of selection at each budget, and each route pays for fresh encoder processing plus any invoked decoder processing.

Centered selection gains 3.6034 F1 points over exact-250-call hash routing ([2.1127,5.2207][2.1127,5.2207]) but uses 3.69% more service, since equal call counts can still select different input lengths. It saves 28.00% service over always-Prefill1 while losing 4.0956 F1 points. The centered rule’s DEV advantage over Abs0 does not carry over: Abs0 obtains 91.0268 F1 with 216 calls and 31.5589 seconds, compared with 90.3795, 250, and 34.1989 for centered routing. Centered q10/q50 yield 88.0069/93.3937 F1 and 26.4375/40.3954 seconds; we retain the predefined primary budget rather than replacing it with q50. Thus the simpler rule is preferable on this cohort, even though selection improves on random allocation at matched calls. Appendices C.1 and C.2 report development, the complete quality–cost frontier, and the adverse tail-latency results.

5.4 Choosing what verification should return

In a developer dashboard, the verifier receives a completed report and the logs or documents available to the assistant, then flags reports for inspection. Checking a claim that all tests passed against a supplied failure log needs an alarm without enumerating every erroneous quotation. A screen that highlights the offending words also needs localization; complete spans and categories provide a fuller account. The flag helps prioritize inspection without requiring every flagged report to be discarded or every unflagged report to be accepted.

The first-quotation experiment measures the cost of recovering a pointer and the locations it misses. An alarm alone cannot locate or repair an error, so its service time should be compared only with methods returning the same required information. A later localization pass adds cost. Model selection offers a separate choice: the optimized encoder is faster and escalation adds generator calls, whereas native readouts change the output read from a fixed model. Applications requiring locations should use the localization measurements.

6 Related Work

Grounded verification at different granularities.

RAGTruth annotates hallucinations at word level in naturally generated responses (Niu et al., 2024). MiniCheck studies efficient document-grounded fact checking (Tang et al., 2024), while LettuceDetect and Luna use compact encoders to localize unsupported content (Kovács and Recski, 2025; Belyi et al., 2025). The code, tool-output, and structured-document evaluation of Kovács et al. (2026) supplies our benchmark and both checkpoints. It already reports span- and example-level F1. We use those same references to compare the output read from a fixed verifier, measuring its service cost and the functionality retained. Scores from other source mixtures do not provide head-to-head comparisons for this question.

Early verification and short decisions.

PrefixNLI trains entailment models on incomplete answer prefixes to provide feedback during generation (Harary et al., 2026). Our answer is complete before verification starts; we shorten the verifier’s output. Gabriel (2026) estimates correctness confidence from first-content-token entropy in closed-book factual QA. Here the decision comes from the learned structural branch of a context-grounded detector. Reasoning’s Razor compares reasoning modes with classification-prefilled prompts and normalized label-token scores (Chegini et al., 2026). Our prefix preserves the detector’s native span format, and the decision is an unrestricted greedy continuation at its list branch.

Structured decoding and model allocation.

Assistant continuation makes prefix input possible (Hugging Face, 2026). SGLang’s compressed finite-state machines use it to jump over deterministic portions of structured output (Zheng et al., 2024). We build on this syntax-skipping principle by identifying where a native span detector has already supplied an alarm. The experiments measure its increment over ordinary early stopping, with official/raw full readouts and evidence and localization controls. The auxiliary routing study follows confidence-based model allocation in FrugalGPT and AutoMix (Chen et al., 2024; Aggarwal et al., 2024). It combines the optimized encoder with a native-alarm call and records the resulting service cost, including the simpler gate’s stronger transfer.

7 Conclusion

The frozen span verifier studied here commits to an alarm before generating an error description. Reading that branch avoids localization work; supplying its fixed syntax as input also avoids serial formatting decisions. Both changes retain the native instruction. On code-agent TEST, Prefill1 reduces eager resident service by 84.84% relative to full generation and by 31.98% relative to eight-token stopping. The latter saving is 6.74–26.73% under default compiled execution on the complete workload, with corresponding F1 changes of −0.12-0.12 to +0.27+0.27 points. Actual execution affects both cost and individual decisions. Early stopping accounts for most of the reduction; prefilling provides an additional gain whose size depends on the runtime. Comparing only against full output would conflate these two sources of savings.

First-quotation decoding reduces matched service by 51.94% relative to full output while retaining all raw alarms, but loses 0.59 points of offset F1. Full generation supplies the remaining descriptions. A caller can choose the readout for the output it needs, alongside its choice of detector and execution setting.

Limitations

We study one frozen 2B checkpoint with a specified native grammar. The conditional identity assumes that ordinary generation emits the supplied prefix under identical computation. Kernels, batch shapes, and finite precision can violate that computational match, and the empirical comparisons report the resulting decision changes. Bootstrap intervals describe uncertainty conditional on the fixed outputs and source grouping; they do not establish population equivalence.

Quality is measured against released span references whose precision varies by source. Both models trained on unified TRAIN. DEV was exposed, and later functional/runtime controls reuse closed inputs. The additional cohort is upstream validation used to select the encoder checkpoint; the generator’s selection rule is unspecified. Lexical closure reduces overlap but does not certify semantic or repository independence, or rule out contamination during model training.

An alarm provides neither locations nor categories, and the first quotation gives incomplete localization. The evidence intervention uses constructed literal records. These tests concern the relation between a supplied record and a report, so a successful alarm does not certify program execution, patch success, or every claim in a deployed report. The results apply to the verification requests evaluated here.

Service cost depends on the workload, engine, batching, and measurement boundary. The original batch measurement excludes shared preparation; the later fresh-service measurement includes it. The compiled comparison uses the default optimized execution path and therefore cannot isolate the effect of CUDA Graphs alone. It covers 63 fixed chunks in both orders on one allocation, including reverse service comparisons and small decision changes; startup and capture costs are recorded separately. Batch service, per-request latency, and allocation billing measure different costs. The optimized encoder is faster, and cross-model quality differences also reflect checkpoint capability. Finally, the binary comparison uses one fixed contract on exposed DEV. It is neither a new modern TEST result nor evidence that span training is necessary.

Ethical Considerations

This work uses released data and frozen models. Binary alarms can miss unsupported content or flag supported text and should assist inspection, not certify safety or correctness. Dataset/model rights, sensitive content, and intended artifact licenses require human-author review before external release.

OpenAI Codex assisted with experiment orchestration, analysis, figure preparation. AI tools are not authors. The human authors are responsible for the content, accuracy, attribution, and final approval of this work.
