Appendix A Complete data and execution protocol

A.1 How to reproduce, audit, and adapt the readout

The appendix follows the decisions needed to implement and inspect the method. Section A fixes the input interface, tokenizer/model revisions, prefix, parsing rules, data boundaries, and cost scopes. Section B retains the complete source comparisons, localization measurements, binary-prompt control, and encoder implementations. Section C supplies the optional routing development and all frozen transfer points. The conditional argument and decision-change accounting are in Section D; evidence interventions and all runtime orders are in Section E. Section F adds the semantics-matched binary contract and compiled-execution controls, with their full grammar and cost audits. Section H connects these results to their preserved evidence and complete exploration costs.

To reconstruct the focal inference path, tokenize the unchanged native request containing the evidence and complete answer. For Native8, generate at most eight tokens from that prompt. For Prefill1, append the pinned seven syntax token IDs to the prompt IDs and generate at most one unrestricted greedy token. Decode the generated IDs for Native8, or the concatenation of supplied and generated IDs for Prefill1. At the first JSON object’s hallucinated_spans list, the whitespace-tolerant parser maps ] to no alarm and { to an alarm. A missing or unexpected branch, an empty generation, an exceeded cap, or an unexpected termination remains invalid. The short-output parser does not require completed JSON, and neither readout applies the later quotation-to-offset map. Actual prompt and output IDs are audited independently of this text parser. Decoding skips special tokens and disables tokenization-space cleanup; accepted termination reasons are stop and length. The native request is tokenized once, and prefix IDs are appended without retokenizing the decoded concatenation.

The manuscript source archive contains the text, bibliography, and figures needed to compile the paper. Reproducibility artifacts are maintained separately. The portable core implements full native generation, Native8, and Prefill1, with pinned model and dataset identities, a source adapter, and a CPU scorer. Aggregate CSV tables record the primary readouts, cascades, branch stability, evidence interventions, runtime batches, and interface controls. JSON manifests preserve worker/scorer hashes, protocol identities, corrections, and complete exploration costs. Offline checks reconstruct the primary F1 scores, optimized service totals, and allocation costs from those aggregates. These checks are not a fresh GPU reproduction, and the portable core does not reimplement the auxiliary controls. Model weights, raw benchmark text, evaluator references, and original execution traces are not included in this manuscript-only archive; independent rerunning requires the corresponding pinned assets and execution records.

Adapting the idea to another verifier requires a new native-interface check, not reuse of the number seven. On development data, identify a class-independent prefix followed by a branch that determines the requested output. A rationale or other input-dependent content before that branch cannot simply be supplied as fixed syntax. Freeze the new prefix, parser, caps, and cost scope before comparison on separate inputs; compare full raw, full postprocessed, native early stopping, and supplied-prefix continuation. Preserve invalid branches, all input/output token costs, and any functionality lost by stopping. This procedure describes how to test an extension; the present experiments establish the result for the specified frozen verifier.

A.2 Frozen prefix and routing parameters

For the pinned decoder tokenizer, the seven class-independent syntax IDs are (4754,40839,1692,15025,9823,581,763). The branch follows this exact sequence; the prefix does not include a class-dependent list item or empty-list choice. The fixed native parser accepts an empty-list or first-object branch and retains other continuations as invalid. Actual input/output ID audits check this native interface separately from the quotation-to-offset mapping of complete outputs.

For the later centered cascade, a single full-DEV deployment fit fixes t=−0.935546875t=-0.935546875 and radii r.10=0.541015625r_{.10}=0.541015625, r.25=1.322265625r_{.25}=1.322265625, and r.50=2.384765625r_{.50}=2.384765625. Each radius is the sorted DEV distance at zero-based index ⌊q⁡(n−1)⌋\lfloor q(n-1)\rfloor; all ties escalate. The q25 radius is the primary point. These are development quantiles, not a promise of identical call fractions after transfer.

Let CE​(x)C_{E}(x) and CD​(x)C_{D}(x) include each model’s fresh preparation and service, and let CR​(x)C_{R}(x) denote routing overhead. For gate g⁡(x)g(x) the request cost is Cg​(x)=CE​(x)+g⁡(x)​CD​(x)+CR​(x)C_{g}(x)=C_{E}(x)+g(x)C_{D}(x)+C_{R}(x). Relative to always using the decoder, expected warm cost falls only when

𝔼⁡[(1−g⁡(x))​CD​(x)]>𝔼⁡[CE​(x)+CR​(x)].\mathbb{E}[(1-g(x))C_{D}(x)]>\mathbb{E}[C_{E}(x)+C_{R}(x)].

The condition permits input length and routing to be correlated: call fraction alone cannot determine savings. Shared initialization and qualification are separately charged.

A.3 Development and test boundaries

Table 3 distinguishes the initial evidence stages; the additional README confirmation is reported separately in Section B.4. The Data2txt development cohort was already exposed during method development and is not independent confirmation. It also comes from official TRAIN, which the public models may have seen during their original training. The tool-output test measured the fixed Native8 point before the final shared-engine prefill confirmation. Prefill1 was not run on that tool-output test. The code-agent selection, readouts, caps, scheduling, metrics, and transferred encoder threshold were fixed before the code-agent examples and labels were opened. We evaluate all selected responses, with no class, quality, length, or outcome filtering.

Both initial test sources are from the pinned public release KRLabsOrg/lettucedetect-code-hallucination, revision 866a7c5392c3cf87e4fbc2b3808815d524f54331, under CC BY 4.0 KRLabsOrg (2026a). The exact source selectors are lettucedetect-tool-output and lettucedetect-code-agent. The authors describe model-proposed local edits with edit-derived reference spans and source-based splits; code-agent TEST uses model-assisted triage and author review/adjudication (Kovács et al., 2026, §4.3–4.4). These are released reference spans, not our independent human-gold annotations. We use them without repairs; they do not establish exhaustive execution or real-world correctness.

For the two initial test sources, components close exact normalized nonempty questions or contexts and context near-duplicates with five-word Jaccard similarity at least 0.85. The development source uses its 171 fixed source families, retaining all six sibling answers per family. Source grouping is completed without labels. Two context-near links from the code-agent selection to the previously exposed tool source are recorded and retained; they are not excluded after selection. These rules do not find all semantic duplicates or establish separation from every model-training example.

A.4 Models and the fast learned control

The frozen generative model is the public LettuceDetect Qwen3.5-2B checkpoint, revision 4511d95c6a5f24df1e810a097685d068208cb149. The encoder is the released 307M mmBERT-base counterpart, revision 8831ce063dff760b01efe4519b4188f5ee2456f2. The paper reports that both are trained on the unified task split Kovács et al. (2026). Thus the evaluation is within the authors’ held-out task sources, not unknown-domain or contamination-free zero-shot transfer. The models differ in capacity, objectives, and training recipes; we do not attribute their capability difference to early stopping.

The encoder uses native answer-token argmax and flags a response if any valid answer token is unsupported. We also transfer exactly one previously frozen Data2txt threshold: maxj⁡(ℓj,1−ℓj,0)>−0.9401225447654724\max_{j}(\ell_{j,1}-\ell_{j,0})>-0.9401225447654724. Native and thresholded predictions share the same forward pass. No threshold is fitted on any test source. On DEV, this fixed threshold is an in-sample diagnostic; an earlier FP32 source-fold threshold control obtained 90.45 F1 and is not replaced by that diagnostic.

The encoder follows the public context-only only_first truncation strategy, configured at its 8,192-token capacity rather than the package default 4,096. The full answer IDs and offsets are preserved. Decoder context capacity is 32,768 tokens for both test sources. All overlength encoder contexts remain in the primary evaluation. CPU lengths also prospectively define a secondary subset needing no encoder truncation: 373 tool-output responses in 321 components and 1,574 code-agent responses in 1,189 components. The eligibility rule was fixed before new labels were opened. Actual membership was computed from CPU lengths after local reference projection but before model outputs, without using labels. These subsets do not replace the full cohorts.

A.5 Execution, uncertainty, and cost

The shared-engine DEV and code-agent assays initialize the 2B model once. They process original-order chunks of 32, rotating through three arm orders: Full–Native8–Prefill1, Native8–Prefill1–Full, and Prefill1–Full–Native8. The code-agent assay has 189 generate calls and 6,045 decoder requests. Each arm uses greedy decoding, seed 0, the same checkpoint and native source prompt, and unrestricted vocabulary. Prefix caching is explicitly disabled and its actual configuration is recorded. The main confirmation runs on one NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 (81,559 MiB reported), driver 610.43.02, with vLLM 0.17.1+cu128, Torch 2.10.0, Transformers 4.57.6, and tokenizers 0.22.2. We use eager vLLM execution with at most eight sequences; the fixed interleaving is not repeated randomized latency sampling. The earlier tool-output arms instead run in separate processes, so their individual loading times are shown separately.

The encoder runs once in a separate process, batch size four, in original order with BF16 parameters and logits, FP32 readback, SDPA, and TF32 disabled. We verify its 22 FP32 rotary buffers and effective rotary theta of 160,000. The existing Transformers 4.57.6 compatibility implementation is held fixed. It is not a claim of bitwise identity with the upstream HF5 implementation or a lower bound on optimized encoder runtime.

Saved token IDs, source hashes, actual samplers, model identities, offsets, request counts, and cost records are checked before evaluator labels are parsed. No incomplete arm receives favorable partial-cohort quality scoring. We retain invalid outputs and report invalid-as-negative, invalid-as-positive, and always-wrong sensitivity rules. All focal reported arms have zero invalid decisions and zero unknown request costs, so these rules give the same scores here.

Our main metric is positive-class response F1; accuracy and confusion counts accompany the artifacts. Paired percentile intervals use 2,000 whole-component bootstrap resamples, seed 20261024, shared across contrasts within a cohort. They condition on the frozen model, grouping, and observed run. They do not account for adaptive DEV use, undetected dependence, or training and timing variation, and are not equivalence tests.

Decoder service timers include each chunk’s generation and associated local result handling, excluding shared initialization and source preparation. Engine-call wall time is the narrower generation-call timer, not a direct GPU-kernel profiler. Encoder forward, tokenization, transfer, projection, initialization, and worker times are reported separately. In particular, its worker-minus-initialization timer includes tokenization and is not interchangeable with decoder service time. Main-job GPU seconds are allocation duration times allocated GPUs, counted once, including startup and idle or CPU work during the allocation.

Appendix B Detailed frozen measurements

B.1 Development and tool-output evidence

On exposed DEV (Table 4), Prefill1 is 0.1977 percentage points below Native8 (95% interval [−0.5374,+0.0829][-0.5374,+0.0829]). There are five branch differences, despite every full and native-eight output sharing the fixed first seven IDs. Service time falls from 34.475 to 14.033 seconds; full service takes 189.105 seconds. Shared initialization is 49.633 seconds and complete decoder worker time is 347.999 seconds. The completed allocation costs 352 GPU-seconds. A preserved sampler-guard failure consumed another 64 GPU-seconds before any model call; its runtime-only repair accepted vLLM’s greedy top_k normalization without changing the method.

On the tool-output test, all 617 raw full decisions and actual first eight output IDs match Native8. Worker time falls from 157.121 to 83.543 seconds, a 46.83% reduction, with separate loading times of 54.911 and 36.900 seconds. Worker-minus-loading time is 102.210 versus 46.644 seconds; engine-call time is 84.889 versus 29.833 seconds. These are single process observations.

Official location matching removes one true-positive full prediction. Consequently, Native8 exceeds official full F1 by 0.1806 points, with a component interval of [0,+0.5733][0,+0.5733], while matching raw full exactly. This difference is a postprocessing effect, not evidence that early stopping reasons better. Its gap over the frozen-threshold encoder is 12.35 points ([8.93,15.80][8.93,15.80]); on the 373-response no-truncation subset, the gap is 9.46 points ([5.42,13.86][5.42,13.86]). The encoder takes 106.125 seconds overall, including 19.366 seconds of tokenization and 69.979 seconds of forward calls. The complete three-system allocation costs 440 GPU-seconds.

B.2 Prospective code-agent confirmation

The all-response code-agent results support two distinct efficiency points. Native8 reaches 83.6594 F1 versus official full’s 83.4128. Prefill1 reaches 83.4304, with precision 90.0571%, recall 77.7120%, and accuracy 84.4665%. Its confusion counts are 788 true positives, 87 false positives, 226 false negatives, and 914 true negatives. The corresponding official-full counts are 787, 86, 227, and 915. Aggregate proximity therefore does not mean identical errors.

All 2,015 full and Native8 trajectories have the fixed first seven IDs. Full’s first eight IDs match Native8 on 2,007 responses; reconstructed prefill output also matches Native8 on 2,007. The eight differences in each comparison show why the ideal same-prefix argument is insufficient to infer empirical quality. None of the prefill continuations uses an unexpected diagnostic branch ID, although the decoder was not restricted to those IDs. Full official processing drops 35 span strings overall and changes two positive response decisions relative to raw presence. We retain the official/raw distinction in every comparison.

The same-training encoder obtains 76.5936 F1 by native argmax and 77.3960 using the transferred threshold. It truncates only the context of 441 responses, removing 1,453,394 encoder tokens; answers remain intact. On the prespecified no-truncation subset of 1,574 responses and 1,189 components, full official, Native8, and Prefill1 obtain 82.3939, 82.6389, and 82.5000 F1, while the fixed-threshold encoder obtains 76.5432. The prefill–encoder gap is 5.9568 points ([3.6213,8.2334][3.6213,8.2334]). Thus unequal maximum input capacity alone does not explain the observed model gap. This comparison still does not isolate the causal contribution of capacity, training, or architecture.

B.3 Measured computation and complete costs

Table 6 gives the paired decoder timers. Native8 reduces service by 77.72% relative to full generation. Prefill1 reduces it by 84.84%, or 31.98% relative to Native8. The narrower engine-call reductions are 79.69%, 87.71%, and 39.47%, respectively. These percentages concern the resident decoder’s service, not total job time.

Common decoder initialization takes 74.512 seconds. Source preparation and tokenization take 203.388 seconds, and asset verification takes 3.662 seconds. The full three-arm decoder worker takes 919.893 seconds. Prefill still processes the long evidence. We do not estimate a standalone one-arm deployment time by distributing shared work arbitrarily.

The encoder separately takes 360.969 seconds overall: 11.807 for initialization, 79.818 for tokenization, 234.720 for forward calls, 0.912 for input transfer, and 17.903 for projection and readback, plus remaining verification and bookkeeping. Its worker-minus-initialization time of 349.161 seconds includes tokenization. Comparing that number directly with the decoder’s preparation-excluding 67.668-second service timer would exaggerate a common-scope speed claim. The forward/engine-call timers and complete worker totals are exposed instead of collapsed into one purportedly equivalent latency.

The complete shared-decoder-plus-encoder allocation is 1,296 GPU-seconds, counted once, including startup and CPU work during the allocation. Before allocation, decoder and encoder CPU fit checks take 223.27 and 109.92 seconds; the subsequent CPU ID audit takes 231.60 seconds after GPU release. These are additional CPU costs, outside that GPU duration. None adds a model call. The readouts introduce no paid API, new training, or new weights.

The logical total for Native8 and Prefill1 is exactly 8,621,241 tokens. Prefill adds 14,105 input tokens and removes exactly 14,105 output tokens. Even relative to full, total logical tokens fall by only 0.91%, much less than service time. On tool output the total-token reduction is 0.44%. These quantities demonstrate a change in sequential work, not an equal reduction in a provider’s bill. Encoder and decoder tokens use different tokenizers and are not interchangeable monetary units.

B.4 Prospective developer-document extension

We fixed the same readouts, checkpoints, caps, schedule, and encoder threshold before materializing any README instances or labels. All 641 responses of lettucedetect-readme from the same pinned release remain, grouped into 638 source-derived lexical components. This is a new project-held-out source, within the authors’ task: both public models were trained on its TRAIN. The component count does not establish repository or semantic independence.

All 641 official/raw full decisions, Native8 decisions, and Prefill1 decisions agree. Every native prefix and prefill reconstruction also agrees; these are sample observations, not population equivalence. Prefill1 reduces decoder service by 90.2593% against full and 62.4789% against Native8 (Table 7). All encoder pairs fit without truncation. Its lower F1 therefore cannot be attributed solely to the 8k limit, but the model capability gap remains inherited. The transferred threshold performs worse than native argmax and is retained without refitting.

Shared decoder initialization takes 57.5152 seconds, tokenization/preparation 17.1854, and the complete three-arm worker 207.5509. The encoder’s complete worker takes 19.0449 seconds, including 8.7356 for initialization and 2.0495 for tokenization; its forward calls take 3.1505 seconds. In particular, its 10.3093 seconds excluding initialization still includes preparation and cannot be compared directly with Prefill1’s preparation-excluding 8.3065-second service as a speed win. The combined allocation costs 232 GPU-seconds, counted once; post-release CPU actual-ID auditing takes another 25.697 seconds. Native8 and Prefill1 each use 502,567 logical tokens, versus 516,274 for full: only a 2.655% total-token reduction, without a proportional billing claim.

The released card describes README as lower-precision first-pass edit-derived references, with some errors detectable without context KRLabsOrg (2026a). The code-test per-example review description does not extend to this source. Thus 98.58 F1 is agreement with released references, not independently established real-error accuracy, evidence dependence, contamination-free transfer, or field-wide state of the art. This source is now closed to method tuning.

B.5 An optional first predicted location

On exposed DEV, the fixed FirstQuote rule gives alarm F1 94.3554 versus matched full raw 94.4212, with service 69.070 versus 194.379 seconds (−64.47%-64.47\%). We then transfer that rule unchanged to all 2,015 code-agent responses in 1,613 components. Their earlier outcomes are already known: this is an additional functional comparison, not new independent confirmation or a replacement for Tables 4–6.

Full raw and FirstQuote agree on every response alarm in this run (Table 8). FirstQuote reduces service by 51.9395% and output tokens from 81,036 to 32,606 (−59.7636%-59.7636\%), but total tokens by only 0.55665%; each arm processes 8,619,226 input tokens. This observed agreement does not establish population equivalence.

Location coverage declines: 14 of 875 FirstQuote alarms are unmappable, versus one for full. Among 861 jointly located predictions, 846 quotations and offsets agree and 15 differ; 13 locations are available only after full generation. Offset-presence F1 is 82.8800 versus full official 83.4746, a −0.5946-0.5946-point difference (component interval [−1.0496,−0.2048][-1.0496,-0.2048]). Against released edit-derived spans, first-location micro character precision is 56.6728% versus 56.8585%, and recall over all reference characters is 28.6444% versus 29.1267%. A located quote is a predicted error location, not an entailment certificate or a complete span set.

All 6,045 requests pass the actual-ID/hash audit with zero invalid alarms or unknown costs. Shared initialization is 56.8347 seconds, preparation 228.7269, asset verification 5.3583, and worker time 1,008.4328. The complete allocation costs 1,017 GPU-seconds, counted once; the post-release CPU audit takes 188.2404 seconds. These new matched-run clocks do not replace the prospective main experiment’s costs.

B.6 Bounded warm single-request measurements

We hash-select 18 already exposed Data2txt DEV components and one answer each, without labels. Three rounds per case–arm pair balance all three order positions; a nineteenth component provides one warmup per arm. All 165 calls remain: 162 measured plus three warmup. One resident engine uses maximum sequence count one and no prefix caching. Base input lengths are 938–1,921 tokens (median 1,362); prefill adds seven.

For each case we take each arm’s median over three rounds, divide prefill by native-eight latency, then summarize those 18 ratios by their median, rather than dividing Table 9’s pooled medians. The host-generate ratio is 0.170154 (82.9846% reduction), median paired difference −145.517-145.517 ms; service gives 0.246363 (75.3637%), difference −145.485-145.485 ms. All 54 round-wise triples have valid, agreeing decisions and identical reconstructed eight-token prefixes. This is functional agreement, not new F1 or quality-equivalence evidence.

Host generation times synchronous llm.generate. Service adds actual re-encoding, prompt writing, optional existing-driver-context synchronization, parsing, and completion/prediction writes; it includes the pre-generate inflight-session write but excludes final request/batch/session record commits and does not independently synchronize another process. Shared initialization takes 50.699 seconds, preparation 18.812, verification 4.005, and the complete worker 183.567. Warmup service totals 4.205 seconds; all warmup is charged in 189 GPU-seconds. Subsequent CPU ID auditing takes 19.866 seconds outside that allocation. Eighteen sources, not 54 independent cases, support only this bounded host-clock observation, not production tails, general modern interactive latency, or end-to-end agent latency.

Modern code-agent extension.

We repeat the same finite singleton design on the existing code-agent cohort, with a new fixed hash salt selecting 18 source components, one answer per component, and a nineteenth warmup component. Selection uses only component keys and qids, with no labels, input-length selection, or method changes. The source’s historical quality results are already known; this is an additional timing measurement, not new quality confirmation. We retain all 165 calls and use the original code-agent user wrapper, one resident H100 80GB, maximum sequence count one, 32k context, BF16 eager execution, and no prefix caching. Selected base prompts span 2,478–7,194 tokens (median 4,203), extending beyond the short DEV input range.

The prespecified median of 18 per-qid median-of-three prefill/native-eight ratios is 0.176369 for host generation (82.3631% reduction), with median paired difference −166.345-166.345 ms. Service gives 0.333779 (66.6221%), difference −164.449-164.449 ms. These are paired summaries, distinct from dividing Table 10’s pooled medians. All 54 measured triples have valid, agreeing branch decisions, and all actual full-first-eight/native-eight/prefill-reconstructed IDs agree. This functional observation does not supersede the eight decision changes in the complete 2,015-response batch confirmation or establish equal population quality.

Shared initialization takes 65.283 seconds, tokenization/preparation 24.704 seconds, asset verification 6.888 seconds, and complete worker time 219.625 seconds. All three warmup calls cost 3.970 seconds of service and remain charged in the 225 GPU-second allocation. The subsequent CPU actual-ID audit takes 20.893 seconds after GPU release. Measured native-eight and prefill logical totals are both 240,888 tokens; 378 output positions become input positions. The bounded gain extends to these longer modern inputs; it does not establish cold-start, network, concurrent-service, or complete-agent latency savings.

SDPA encoder singleton control.

We then run the fixed 307M BF16 encoder on exactly these 18 sources and rounds, with the same nineteenth-source warmup: 55 forwards in a separate allocation, without new selection, labels, F1, or fitting. Each binary service call freshly encodes the pair, constructs and transfers tensors, synchronizes the forward, reduces FP32 answer-logit margins on GPU, reads one scalar, and commits a minimal alarm. Native and transferred-threshold decisions share that forward. Full logits, actual IDs/masks, and exact CPU readout checks are recorded outside binary service, with their costs retained.

Encoder median service is 273.088 ms (forward 240.680 ms; encoding 29.073 ms). The prespecified median of 18 per-qid median-of-three encoder/decoder service ratios is 0.536918 against full, 1.080135 against Native8, and 3.205585 against Prefill1; the latter median paired difference is +189.084+189.084 ms. All 55 scalar/full-logit audits agree and all three-round encoder decisions are stable. This locates a useful warm operating point, not new quality confirmation. Four of the 18 encoder contexts are truncated at 8,192 tokens with complete answers retained; tokenizers, backends, allocations, preprocessing, and logging boundaries differ, and historical decoder service includes heavier logging. Encoder loading is shorter: initialization 14.952 s, preparation 0.806 s, assets 1.520 s, warmup service 0.809 s, and worker 35.201 s. Measured diagnostic work adds 0.372 s outside binary service; the whole allocation is 37 GPU-seconds, counted once. These clocks do not establish cold-start or universal dominance.

Attention implementation control.

We reuse the same 18 sources, three rounds, and nineteenth-source warmup in one resident encoder, rotating three fixed implementations (Table 11). All retain the checkpoint, BF16, original QKV and FP32 RoPE, token IDs, answer mask, and 8k context policy. Two project bridges use the installed FA3 kernel, not native HF FlashAttention2: one retains dense-mask construction; the other expresses the same global/local windows directly and skips redundant masks only for these batch-one, all-valid inputs.

The prespecified median paired direct-window/SDPA service ratio is 0.171300. Against historical Prefill1 it is 0.497155, reversing the SDPA speed ordering, subject to the cross-allocation and service-scope differences above. All 54 paired native and frozen-threshold decisions agree across implementations, but margins change on all 18 sources; the two FA3 variants agree with each other. Fixed zero-QK primitives validate window support and normalization, not arbitrary-QK or quality equivalence. Dense-mask host clocks are nested enqueue timings, not additive GPU-kernel profiles. The new allocation costs 70 GPU-seconds once, including diagnostics; initialization takes 28.503 s, preparation 0.998 s, and complete worker time 67.683 s. This bounded timing result does not by itself establish the bridge’s complete-cohort quality.

Complete optimized encoder control.

A separately frozen pass now evaluates the direct-window bridge on all original 2,015 code-agent responses and 1,613 components, in original order, with no labels, fitting, new cases, or decoder replay. Both fixed readouts share each batch-one forward. The same 441 context truncations and all answer IDs/offsets remain. This adds a stronger implementation control on an already exposed test, not independent confirmation.

All 2,015 actual-input, full-logit, scalar, and window-execution audits pass, with no invalid or unknown-cost calls. Relative to cached SDPA, 1,952 margins and 16 native/12 fixed-threshold decisions change; native F1 rises 0.2040 points while fixed-threshold F1 falls 0.0615 points (Table 12). Batch shape and attention arithmetic both differ, so these changes are not attributable solely to the kernel and do not establish quality equivalence. Prefill1 exceeds the optimized fixed-threshold encoder by 6.0958 points (1,613-component 95% interval [4.0262,8.2156][4.0262,8.2156]); on the unchanged 1,574-response no-truncation subset, it obtains 82.5000 versus 76.4602, a 6.0398-point gap ([3.6800,8.3340][3.6800,8.3340]). The fixed-threshold encoder has higher recall (84.12% versus 77.71%); the F1 advantage is not every-metric superiority and remains inherited from the public models.

The new encoder service totals 100.167 s, including 65.800 s of fresh pair encoding and 28.406 s of synchronized forward calls; complete logits/ID diagnostics add a separately measured 15.441 s. Initialization is 21.400 s, assets 2.477 s, and worker time 169.505 s; the complete allocation is 173 GPU-seconds once. Post-release local scoring takes 17.104 s without model calls. These fresh-encoding service totals and the decoder’s preparation-excluding totals have different scopes and cannot be divided into a common-protocol end-to-end speedup. The same-source singleton result instead shows a faster optimized encoder point with lower observed quality than the 2B readout, while the within-2B decoding increment remains.

B.7 Direct one-token binary control on exposed DEV

A shorter direct binary answer is an important simple alternative to native structured readout. We prospectively fix one control on all 1,026 already exposed Data2txt DEV responses (171 source components), using the same frozen 2B checkpoint, facts, user wrapper, and tokenizer. Its shorter system instruction asks for Yes if any answer content is unsupported and No otherwise. Only this control restricts generation to the two exact single-token verbalizers, Yes (ID 9175) and No (ID 2665), with temperature-zero argmax and no fitted threshold. Both actual assistant continuations are CPU-qualified on every input before model construction. The native readouts remain unmasked. No closed test is used to select or optimize the control.

All 3,078 requests and 99 rotating batch calls complete. Binary1 predicts only 12 positive responses: 11 true positives and one false positive, with 704 false negatives and recall 1.54%. Its shorter input costs 1,131,895 tokens, versus 1,471,501 for Prefill1; both generate 1,026 tokens. It saves 1.004 seconds of service relative to Prefill1 at unusable detection quality (Table 13). Thus enforcing a valid answer format does not make this direct-prompt transfer task-competent. This fixed recipe is closed; it does not show that binary classification or every binary prompt is weak.

Within this run, Prefill1 reduces service by 61.52% against Native8, with F1 lower by 0.1317 points (171-component interval [−0.4156,+0.1436][-0.4156,+0.1436]). All native outputs share the fixed first seven IDs; four reconstructed prefill trajectories differ. Shared initialization takes 66.884 seconds, tokenizer/preparation clock 56.772 seconds (including 23.393 seconds for tokenizer initialization), and asset verification 4.075 seconds. Per-arm preparation takes 10.860/11.546/10.972 seconds; these nested clocks are not added again. The complete worker takes 230.005 seconds and allocation 236 GPU-seconds; subsequent CPU ID auditing takes 48.223 seconds after GPU release. Native8 remains the strongest useful same-model short-output control. This format-sensitive result supports reusing the learned native branch, without isolating a causal role for localization training.

B.8 Observed length dependence

A posthoc, zero-model-call analysis retains all 63 paired code-agent chunks, including the final 31-response chunk. The prefill/native-eight engine-call ratio correlates with mean prompt length (tie-aware Spearman 0.923; service 0.881). Four fixed length-rank bins have median generation ratios 0.5665, 0.5969, 0.6389, and 0.6673: relative savings decrease with length. Generation is faster in all 63 chunks; service in 62, retaining one ratio-2.411 outlier. Arm-position summaries vary much less. This is consistent with prompt work amortizing saved serial decode steps, but it remains observational rather than causal or kernel-level evidence; it does not explain cross-workload differences by length alone.

Appendix C Auxiliary encoder-to-generator routing

This extension was explored after the structural-readout study. It reuses the frozen models and is not a new routing algorithm: confidence and verification cascades have established precedents (Chen et al., 2024; Aggarwal et al., 2024). We retain it as an auxiliary detector-specific allocation point rather than the premise of the main contribution.

Frozen gate and strong control.

On the exposed Data2txt development set, a response escalates to Prefill1 when the absolute native encoder margin is no larger than a fixed cutoff. Five whole-source hash folds retain cutoffs selected from the old SDPA training folds: 1.2890625, 1.205078125, 1.236328125, 1.17578125, and 1.244140625. The subsequent FA3 implementation does not refit them. Unescalated predictions use the sole old-DEV threshold −0.9401225447654724-0.9401225447654724. The control uses the same calibrated encoder and exactly the same escalation count in each fold, choosing the smallest fixed-salt identifier hashes. All contrasts preserve all responses; there is no budget, salt, seed, or target-threshold search. The calibrated hash is the relevant strong control, rather than a weaker native-zero fallback.

Actual development services.

One allocation keeps both models resident on one GPU, with a fixed 0.70 vLLM memory share, one active decoder sequence, BF16 precision, and no prefix cache. A separately charged label-free encoder pass freezes actual per-fold counts and hash routes before any new decoder output. Three policies then alternate in original row order. Both cascade policies pay fresh encoder tokenization, transfer, forward, FP32 margin projection, and routing on every response, including non-escalated responses. Only escalated cases additionally pay fresh decoder tokenization/generation/parsing. Always-prefill pays only its own required stages. All policies stop their service clocks after the same minimal alarm write and fsync. Full-logit/ID diagnostics, source qualification, initialization, probe, warmup, and cleanup are charged separately; they are not declared saved by the route.

Uncertainty exceeds the calibrated equal-call hash by 0.7453 F1 points (conditional component interval [−0.2544,+1.8748][-0.2544,+1.8748]), while its service total is nearly the same. Against always-Prefill1, it loses 1.8817 F1 points ([−2.8047,−0.9790][-2.8047,-0.9790]) and reduces aggregate service by 36.1279% (ratio 0.638721, interval [0.607873,0.670705][0.607873,0.670705]). Its descriptive p95 service is worse, 67.047 versus 53.677 ms, despite a lower median. Uncertainty yields 645/34/70/277 TP/FP/FN/TN, versus 660/63/55/248 for hash: precision improves but recall falls. Neither equal quality nor tail-latency dominance follows.

Both routed policies make 252 actual calls (24.5614%), with no route drift, invalid decisions, unknown costs, or audit issues. Relative to the old SDPA cache, 962 encoder margins and eight native/four calibrated decisions change; actual always-Prefill1 differs from its old cache on three decisions. The actual counts and quality therefore do not substitute cached values. All 1,531 actual decoder calls pass the post-release CPU ID audit. The full allocation is 327 GPU-seconds, including both initializations (58.4077+2.2011 s), preflight (12.9608 s), assets (5.6857 s), probe service (21.9523 s), warmups, diagnostics, planning, primitives, and cleanup; worker time is 324.3946 s. Fewer decoder calls do not imply proportional billed GPU savings.

An initial local validator used encoder-style compact JSON hashing for the decoder’s native prompt-ID serialization and refused all calls before parsing labels. A separately frozen scorer corrects only that serialization expression. The original source, refusal, repair record, and raw outputs remain; no method, mask, metric, data, or model call was changed.

Fixed modern transfer replay.

The entire gate is transferred once to the already evaluated code-agent cohort using its qualified FA3 margins and original Prefill1 decisions. No code-agent quantile is fitted. This is a CPU combination of existing outputs, not actual cascade execution or new independent confirmation.

The route exceeds equal-call hash by 2.8239 F1 points ([1.3801,4.3363][1.3801,4.3363]), calibrated encoder by 4.7114 ([3.1638,6.2716][3.1638,6.2716]), and falls below always-Prefill1 by 1.3845 ([−2.8190,+0.0376][-2.8190,+0.0376]). All 596 planned escalations (29.5782%) use unchanged cutoffs and salts. Uncertainty and hash share 194 escalations and each has 402 unique ones. Their TP/FP/FN/TN are 786/116/228/885 and 835/259/179/742. As on DEV, precision and recall trade off. This replay takes 3.3197 CPU seconds, with zero new model calls, GPU seconds, or API expenditure.

Actual modern cascade services.

A subsequently completed fixed assay executes all three policies on the same 2,015 code-agent responses and 1,613 components (Table 16). It retains the DEV gate, threshold, salts, all 441 encoder context truncations, and complete answers; no new code-agent threshold or budget is fitted. A label-free FA3 probe fixes the actual per-fold counts and hash routes before any new decoder output. Both models remain resident under the same fixed memory share as the DEV assay, and policies rotate once per response in original order. Both routed policies pay fresh encoder processing and routing on every response, with fresh decoder processing only when escalated; always-Prefill1 pays its own required stages. The shared service boundary includes encoding, transfer, required forwards, readout, routing, parsing, and minimal alarm writing/fsync. This is actual execution on a previously exposed cohort, not new independent confirmation.

Uncertainty exceeds calibrated equal-call hash by 2.8239 F1 points (1,613-component conditional 95% interval [1.3801,4.3363][1.3801,4.3363]) at almost identical service: the ratio is 1.001237 ([0.969791,1.031352][0.969791,1.031352]), so the route is not faster than hash. Against actual always-Prefill1, uncertainty loses 1.4461 F1 points ([−2.8776,−0.0135][-2.8776,-0.0135]), while reducing aggregate service by 6.3178% (ratio 0.936822, [0.912262,0.959927][0.912262,0.959927]). This is a smaller measured saving than DEV’s 36.1279%, despite 70.4218% fewer decoder calls. Fresh encoder work and the escalated decoder work both count. Uncertainty precision/recall are 87.1397/77.5148%, versus hash’s 76.3254/82.3471%; the precision gain retains a recall loss. Descriptive service p95 is worse than always-Prefill1, 165.158 versus 125.966 ms. Intervals use 2,000 shared component resamples (seed 20261025) and condition on this one host/pass, actual routes, and frozen outputs; they do not estimate repeated scheduling uncertainty or production tails.

The probe exactly preserves the cached FA3 margins and both encoder readouts. Actual routes match all planned routes. Uncertainty and hash retain their replay confusion counts; actual always-Prefill1 changes one cached decision, adding one true positive (789/87/225/914 TP/FP/FN/TN). Its new 83.4921 F1 is therefore reported with the new clock rather than substituting the main experiment’s 83.4304 F1. All 8,062 requests complete, including 2,015 probe requests, 6,045 policy requests, and two warmups, with 6,046 encoder forwards. All 3,208 decoder calls, including warmup, pass the post-release CPU actual-ID audit in 88.452 s; frozen local scoring adds 21.991 CPU seconds without model calls.

The complete allocation costs 999 GPU-seconds once (worker 994.4089 s), including decoder/encoder initialization (60.7167/2.2613 s), tokenization preflight (67.7822 s), assets (5.7789 s), label-free probe service/diagnostics (98.4331/12.9180 s), encoder/decoder warmup service (0.3526/3.2833 s), full-ID/logit diagnostics for the three policies (4.7253/13.5760/14.1633 s), planning (0.1955 s), primitive qualification (0.1687 s), and cleanup (1.1380 s). These phases are retained separately rather than counted as warm deployment savings; nested clocks are not added again. With both models resident in one allocation, we do not manufacture per-policy GPU bills or infer billed savings from call counts. The useful increment is better allocation of the existing detector’s capability than equal-call hash, with a measured quality–service tradeoff against always-Prefill1. This auxiliary result does not alter the native-readout contribution or establish quality equivalence or field-wide state of the art.

C.1 Centered routing: development and runtime isolation

Exploratory source-fold development.

All measurements in this subsection use the exposed Data2txt DEV cohort: 1,026 responses in 171 whole-source families. The five-fold replay fits each held-out fold’s response threshold by training-fold F1, breaking ties toward the largest threshold. It computes the routing radii on those training folds, then applies the unchanged recipe to the held-out source families. The hash controls share the calibrated fallback and match each route’s actual number of calls within its held-out fold. Table 17 retains all three prespecified budgets and both gates; the 25% point was primary before this measurement. The source and cached predictions were already exposed, so this is exploratory source-fold development rather than new independent confirmation. The replay has no new model calls or service measurement.

At the primary point, centered routing exceeds its equal-call hash by 2.8054 F1 points (171-component conditional 95% interval [1.7168,3.8944][1.7168,3.8944]) and Abs0 by 1.6933 points ([0.5498,2.8316][0.5498,2.8316]), while making 250 versus Abs0’s 254 planned calls. It remains 0.9040 points below always-Prefill1 ([−1.6698,−0.1972][-1.6698,-0.1972]). The 50% point slightly exceeds the always-generator point in this replay, but is retained as a prespecified sensitivity point rather than chosen as the primary budget after inspection. The intervals condition on the fixed exploratory fold predictions and do not refit calibration within each bootstrap sample.

Physical deployment-fit assay.

The deployment threshold −0.935546875-0.935546875 and centered radius 1.3222656251.322265625 are fit once on all exposed DEV. This changes the estimation scope: the resulting physical quality is in-sample and must not replace the source-fold result above. An uncentered 25% radius is 1.2578125, with the same new calibrated fallback; it is distinct from the historical five-cutoff gate. A separately charged label-free encoder probe fixes the source-fold hash routes before any decoder output. Six policy arms then rotate once per original-order response in one co-resident allocation.

The five primary runtime arms share the same single-fresh preparation for each required model. A sixth centered arm retains the earlier preparation path, including full/effective encoder qualification and decoder decode–re-encode checking inside service. The fast path performs those qualification and identity checks outside its service clock, retains their costs, and freshly tokenizes each invoked model inside service. It does not reuse model-input IDs. This isolates preparation overhead from a change in the routing rule or model capability.

With 257 actual calls each, centered routing exceeds hash by 2.4138 F1 points ([1.2859,3.5276][1.2859,3.5276]) and Abs0 by 1.8120 ([0.9020,2.7125][0.9020,2.7125]). Against always-Prefill1, its F1 is 0.2132 points lower ([−0.8614,0.4301][-0.8614,0.4301]), while complete warm service falls 35.2897%: ratio 0.647103 ([0.620627,0.673513][0.620627,0.673513]). This observed small quality difference does not establish quality equivalence. Centered routing is slightly slower in total than Abs0 (ratio 1.004939) and matched hash (1.000791). Against always-encoder, it gains 3.6288 F1 points ([2.5177,4.7651][2.5177,4.7651]) while using 53.7311% more warm service. Its precision is 94.0111%, below Abs0’s 94.8454%, and recall is 94.4056%, above Abs0’s 90.0699%.

The centered fast and old-preparation arms agree on all 1,026 encoder input IDs, margins, routes, and final decisions, and on the prompt/generated IDs of their 257 invoked decoder calls. Changing preparation reduces service 30.2876 to 26.2490 s, or 13.3343% (ratio 0.866657, interval [0.861131,0.873117][0.861131,0.873117]). This isolates runtime overhead in this assay and supplies no new learned capability. Centered service median is 16.749 ms versus always-Prefill1’s 39.068 ms, but its descriptive p95 is worse: 56.924 versus 45.427 ms. All intervals use 2,000 paired whole-family resamples and condition on the fitted deployment policy, actual outputs, and one host/pass; they do not establish repeated-scheduling uncertainty or production-tail behavior.

Complete costs and retained failures.

All 7,184 requests complete: 6,156 measured policy requests, 1,026 probe requests, and two warmups. They invoke 6,157 encoder forwards and 2,055 decoder generations, with zero invalid decisions, unknown costs, or route drift. All 2,055 actual decoder calls pass the independent CPU ID audit. Shared decoder/encoder initialization takes 58.650/2.335 s, within-worker native-ID qualification 28.954 s, asset verification 5.417 s, label-free probe service 18.075 s, planning 0.048 s, and window primitives 0.172 s. The six arms’ full-logit/ID diagnostics add 30.026 s outside their warm service; probe and warmup diagnostics, source preparation, final flushing, and cleanup remain recorded. These are measured stage boundaries, not a selective per-policy share of common cost.

The worker lasts 474.582 s and its complete allocation costs 479 actual GPU-seconds, counted once. Subsequent CPU ID auditing and scoring remain outside that allocation. At this assay’s closure, the complete exploration ledger contains 114 terminal allocations and 84,690 actual GPU-seconds (23.525 GPU-hours), including earlier failures and idle/startup work; API expenditure remains USD 0. The 35.29% warm-service reduction cannot be applied to this whole-job or project total as a GPU, monetary, or energy saving. Two local staging checks stopped before job submission; their records remain and neither consumed a GPU allocation. All historical uncentered results, adverse outcomes, and draft versions are preserved.

C.2 Prospective modern confirmation of the complete policy matrix

Selection and reference boundary.

Before the new source strings or labels were materialized, selection fixed all 1,117 responses from the code-agent, developer-tool-output, and README sources of the same pinned release’s validation split. Source-only closure joined normalized exact question/context matches, context near-duplicates with five-word Jaccard similarity at least 0.85, and whitelisted instance/document identities. It also linked against the already exposed DEV and three historical modern TEST cohorts, reusing their components. Seven tool responses in five components link to the earlier tool cohort; all remain in execution and the complete secondary evaluation. The fixed project-unlinked primary contains 1,110 responses in 639 components. No reference, prediction, length, or observed outcome determined these populations.

Table 19 retains all source counts. These units are a conservative lexical/instance/document closure, not proof of semantic or repository independence. Tool records have no qualified identity field under the fixed projection. Upstream mmBERT checkpoint selection explicitly used development hallucinated-token F1 (Kovács et al., 2026, Section 6.1); the encoder comparison therefore reuses upstream development. The generator’s analogous selection rule is unspecified. This is project-unopened validation rather than a contamination-free external test. Its machine-generated references do not inherit the release’s individual review claim for code-agent TEST; README remains lower-precision edit-derived evidence. All labels are the original released span lists, with exact integer bounds checked. Their presence is the response target, without a new factual-truth or entailment adjudication.

Frozen deployment and common service.

The complete eleven-arm assay uses the fixed DEV threshold −0.935546875-0.935546875, centered radii 0.541015625/1.322265625/2.3847656250.541015625/1.322265625/2.384765625 for the prespecified 10/25/50% DEV quantiles, and uncentered radius 1.25781251.2578125. No modern quantile or threshold is fitted. Each hash route matches its centered route’s decoder count within source, existing component hash-fold, and exposure-status strata. The exposure stratum makes matching hold in both the primary and complete populations. The primary operating point remains Centered25 even when a sensitivity point looks better.

One H100 allocation keeps the unchanged 2B decoder and optimized BF16 FA3 encoder resident. All eleven arms freshly prepare each required model through the same helper, with one active decoder sequence, 32k decoder capacity, no prefix cache, seed zero, and unrestricted greedy decoding. Full/native-eight/ prefill caps are 1,024/8/1. The encoder retains its 8k context-only truncation and complete answer offsets. A separately paid full encoder probe makes the label-free hash plan durable before decoder output; the eleven policy orders then rotate once per original-order response. Fresh services include required encoding, transfer, forward/generation, readout, routing, parsing, and minimal alarm write/fsync. Warmup, initialization, full qualification, probe, detailed diagnostics, final flushing, and cleanup retain separate clocks and remain paid in the allocation.

Complete quality and native readout.

Table 20 reports precision, recall, and response F1 for every native view and all three routed budgets, on both populations. The calibrated fallback is the same for Abs0, centered, and hash arms. Native zero is also reported from the unchanged encoder forward; on the primary its 85.5072 F1 is higher than the transferred DEV-threshold encoder’s 85.0168. Thus the calibrated fallback does not dominate even this simple alternative on the new distribution.

On the primary, Prefill1 has 94.4751 F1 versus full official 94.4547 and native-eight/raw full 94.5522. Its differences are +0.0204+0.0204 points against full official and −0.0770-0.0770 against native-eight. Shared complete fresh service falls 827.4728 to 47.4990 s against full (94.2597%) and 210.7107 to 47.4990 s against native-eight (77.4577%). Table 22 gives conditional component intervals, rather than an equivalence claim. The primary Prefill1 confusion counts are 513/19/41/537 TP/FP/FN/TN; full official has 511/17/43/539. Similar aggregate F1 therefore retains changed errors.

Across all 1,117 responses, full raw and native-eight decisions agree exactly, and all native-eight outputs retain the fixed seven syntax IDs. Prefill changes three native-eight decisions. Official quote-to-offset mapping changes one full raw decision; the complete full run maps 820 quotation spans and drops seven unmappable spans, with zero unparseable full outputs. These are parser/trajectory observations, not proof of entailment. The eight-token and one-token cap hits are intended readout limits; no full generation reaches its 1,024-token cap. There are zero invalid decisions, unknown request costs, or route drifts in the completed matrix, so the three invalid-handling sensitivity rules agree.

Primary routing result and the negative transfer.

Centered25 obtains 90.3795 F1 with 250 calls, versus exact-call Hash25’s 86.7761: +3.6034+3.6034 points, interval [2.1127,5.2207][2.1127,5.2207]. It also increases service 32.9830 to 34.1989 s (ratio 1.036865). Against always-Prefill1, it loses 4.0956 F1 points while reducing warm service 28.0009% (ratio 0.719991). Against calibrated encoder it gains 5.3627 points while using 47.7875% more service. All of these costs include the fresh encoder on every routed-policy response.

The important counterexample is the simpler Abs0 control. It reaches 91.0268 F1 with only 216 calls and 31.5589 s. Centered25 is 0.6473 F1 points lower and 8.3651% slower, while making 34 more calls. Centering therefore does not transfer as an F1–service improvement over this strong control, despite its positive DEV result and advantage over random hash allocation. Its precision/recall of 88.4283/92.4188% differs from Abs0’s 93.3586/88.8087%: a recall increase carries a substantial precision cost. This negative transfer is retained rather than repaired by choosing another threshold, source, or budget.

Centered10 and Centered50 remain prespecified curve points, with 88.0069/93.3937 F1, 102/413 calls, and 26.4375/40.3954 s respectively. Both exceed their equal-call hashes, but the 50% point does not replace the primary 25% point after outcomes. Centered50 still trails always-Prefill1 in pooled F1. Table 21 gives actual costs and tails for the complete matrix.

Prefill1 improves its primary median/p95 service to 36.853/75.482 ms versus native-eight and full, but the routed policy does not dominate it on tails: Centered25 p95 is 94.102 ms. Centered50’s p95 is 105.891 ms. The complete table retains these adverse values rather than inferring tails from average call reduction.

Primary native-eight and prefill each consume exactly 2,391,172 logical decoder input-plus-output tokens: prefill transfers 7,770 tokens from output to input. Across all responses the equal total is 2,413,728, with 7,819 transferred tokens. In contrast, primary Centered25 sums to 3,190,274 logical positions across both models, 33.4188% above always-prefill’s decoder positions despite its lower measured service. Models have different sizes, so this unweighted sum is not a FLOP comparison; neither call nor token count establishes allocated-GPU, API-price, or energy savings.

Source heterogeneity, with every source retained.

The pooled primary contains 687 README responses. Tables 23–25 therefore show all source-specific precision/recall/F1 points, not just the pooled score. Code and README have no exposure-linked exclusions, so their primary and complete source evaluations are identical. The tool table gives both the primary 233 and complete 240 responses. Table 26 retains source-specific calls and complete warm service.

The centered primary policy is not uniformly better than Abs0: code F1 is 80.8081 versus 82.1622, README 94.9153 versus 96.0699, and tool 84.5815 versus 82.2967. Centered25 uses more calls than Abs0 in each source. Its code service (11.0650 s) is already close to always-prefill (11.1453 s). Thus a pooled gain over hash does not establish a universal routing upgrade. The predeclared Centered50 point has higher observed tool F1 than always-prefill, while its pooled F1 remains lower; that source-specific observation is reported without a post-hoc policy or source choice.

Prospectively defined no-truncation secondary.

The encoder truncates 131 contexts in all 1,117 responses and truncates no answer. The fixed primary no-encoder-truncation subset contains 979 responses/514 components and 485 released positives. Table 27 reports every readout and budget there. Prefill F1 is 95.4879 versus the calibrated encoder’s 86.3724 and native encoder’s 87.2951, so the inherited capability gap is not explained only by the encoder context limit. Centered25 remains below Abs0 (91.6583 versus 92.3400), with more calls and service.
