Appendix D Conditional prefix stability and finite-sample accounting

Conditional causal-prefix lemma.

Let g⁡(p)g(p) be a deterministic greedy next-token rule for complete token prefix pp, including a fixed rule for breaking ties. Suppose an ordinary native run from pp generates syntax prefix ss. If a prefilled run starts from the identical complete prefix p∥sp\mathbin{\|}s and evaluates the same next-token function, with identical inference arithmetic and relevant state, its continuation equals the ordinary run’s continuation. The first next-token argument is identical; induction applies after each common next token. Therefore a parser determined by this prefix and next token returns the same branch under these premises. This is a conditional identity, not a guarantee that two GPU execution paths compute identical logits or that a generated output is factually correct.

A sufficient numerical condition.

At an identical complete prefix, let ℓ\ell and ℓ~\widetilde{\ell} be two finite all-vocabulary logit vectors with ∥ℓ−ℓ~∥∞≤ϵ\lVert\ell-\widetilde{\ell}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\epsilon. If the original top-one versus runner-up gap exceeds 2​ϵ2\epsilon, the top token cannot change: the top logit can fall by at most ϵ\epsilon, and every competing logit can rise by at most ϵ\epsilon. This condition must hold at each relevant continuation prefix for a longer common trajectory. Our closed traces do not contain all-vocabulary logits and provide neither an empirical ϵ\epsilon nor a numerical certificate from this condition. Token agreement alone does not estimate either quantity.

Exact F1-change bounds without individual labels.

Consider nn responses with PP positive reference labels and Boolean positive prediction sets AA and BB. Partition the responses into C=A∩BC=A\cap B, EA=A∖BE_{A}=A\setminus B, EB=B∖AE_{B}=B\setminus A, and O=(A∪B)cO=(A\cup B)^{c}, with respective sizes mC,mA,mB,mOm_{C},m_{A},m_{B},m_{O}. Let xjx_{j} be the number of positive labels in group jj. These integers satisfy 0≤xj≤mj0\leq x_{j}\leq m_{j} and ∑jxj=P\sum_{j}x_{j}=P. Define α=2/(P+|A|)\alpha=2/(P+|A|) and β=2/(P+|B|)\beta=2/(P+|B|), assigning coefficient zero when its denominator is zero, consistently with zero F1 for that degenerate case. Then

F1​(B)−F1​(A)=(β−α)​xC−α​xA+β​xB.F_{1}(B)-F_{1}(A)=(\beta-\alpha)x_{C}-\alpha x_{A}+\beta x_{B}. (3)

Thus the coefficients for (C,EA,EB,O)(C,E_{A},E_{B},O) are (β−α,−α,β,0)(\beta-\alpha,-\alpha,\beta,0). The exact maximum follows by filling PP integer label units into groups in descending coefficient order, up to each capacity; ascending order gives the exact minimum. If a lower-coefficient group contains a unit while a higher-coefficient group has capacity, transferring that unit cannot decrease the objective, proving the extremal construction. Every feasible integer group allocation is realized by some assignment of labels to the responses, so both endpoints are attainable. The procedure uses only n,P,|A|,|B|n,P,|A|,|B|, and |A∩B||A\cap B|, without individual reference labels.

This bound is finite-sample accounting rather than a confidence interval or a population quality-equivalence test. Individual released labels are used separately to attribute observed true-positive and false-positive changes and to locate the observed difference inside the bound. The analysis retains every previously fixed population. Unknown outputs are reported and do not trigger case deletion to obtain a Boolean-bound result. Few changing predictions can mechanically limit F1 changes; this does not establish evidence dependence, entailment, real-error accuracy, or newly acquired model ability.

Observed branch and mapping attribution.

This additional analysis reuses the closed modern confirmation outputs; it adds no model calls. All nine previously fixed populations remain. In the primary 1,110 responses, the full generation’s first-eight-token branch and its final raw-list alarm agree on every response. The official offset mapper separately removes one true positive, changing F1 by −0.097456-0.097456 points. Native-eight and syntax-prefill differ on only three responses, all negative-to-positive: one additional true positive and two additional false positives. Their observed F1 difference is −0.077032-0.077032 points. Given only the population positive count and these prediction-set sizes/overlap, the exact attainable range is [−0.269866,+0.552486][-0.269866,+0.552486] points. This explains why few altered alarms can bound a small aggregate quality change. Evidence conditioning is examined separately in the fixed intervention assay; the paired intervals describe this finite prediction comparison. The original code-agent trajectory differences and every adverse transfer result are unchanged.

Appendix E Evidence interventions and balanced runtime controls

Upstream development exposure and reference provenance.

The additional modern cohort is project-unopened validation, not a clean external test. In Section 6.1, Kovács et al. (2026) explicitly select the mmBERT checkpoint by development hallucinated-token F1 on the upstream unified split. The encoder is therefore upstream development-exposed on this partition, even though our cohort selection, source closure, and comparison were fixed before our project inspected its responses or labels. The cited paper does not specify an analogous checkpoint-selection rule for Qwen3.5-2B, and we do not extend the encoder attribution to that generator. Section 8 also distinguishes the model-assisted author review of code-agent TEST from automatically checked injection labels in development and the non-code test sources. Released span-list presence therefore defines a common, reproducible quality target for every readout under this annotation provenance.

Scope of the controlled evidence-balance assay.

Our separate construction crosses two recorded target-field values with two fixed literal-value responses in each of 24 tool-return families, retaining all 96 combinations. Each exact response and each exact context occurs once with each label within its family. Excluding opaque identifiers, a classifier that sees only the response or only the context has at most 50% empirical accuracy on this complete balanced pool. Labels are checked by parsing the rendered JSON target field and the literal in the rendered response, rather than by assuming a real tool was executed. This removes one-sided label imbalance and permits a bounded test of whether a frozen readout changes correctly with the supplied fact. The measured readout decisions are evaluated against this literal-consistency target. The complete crossed pool identifies whether decisions respond to the supplied value; its unit of construction is the tool-return family, with four dependent inputs per family.

Prospective evidence-intervention protocol.

Four fixed fixtures in each of six developer-tool domains supply 24 families: failed-test count, command exit code, file count, configuration scalar, artifact path, and a Git field. A family has two JSON target-field values and two responses asserting the corresponding literal values. Crossing them yields two supported and two unsupported responses. The request, distractor fields, and response wording remain fixed when the target value is changed; complete answers remain fixed within the evidence-flip pairs. All 24 quartets, 48 fixed-answer pairs, and 96 inputs remain, including any failures. Opaque identifiers are not supplied to the detector. The unchanged native wrapper receives the complete supplied record and answer, without the local evaluator’s labels or latent states. No model output was inspected to select a fixture, prefix, prompt, threshold, or additional sample.

The frozen full, native-eight, and syntax-prefill readouts each run once on every input, with arm order rotated by input index, under the single-sequence engine. Full raw-list and official-offset alarms reuse the same full generation. Primary summaries are the number of completely correct quartets and the number of fixed-answer pairs for which both evidence states receive the correct opposite judgments. Accuracy, F1, confusion, every domain, invalid-output sensitivities, and readout disagreements accompany those family/pair summaries. These deliberately constructed families are the measurement units; they are not 96 randomly sampled independent natural reports.

Fixed source-only runtime selection.

The separate timing pool reuses 24 previously closed natural responses without reading their quality labels, predictions, or measured times. Within each of the three modern source types, eligible project-unlinked rows are ranked by the untruncated encoder-pair token count and identifier. Each length quartile contributes two fixed-salt hash-selected rows in distinct source components. All 24 are retained and interleaved into three fixed batches of eight. The selection length is a source-only stratifier, not the decoder’s token count. Their prior use precludes a new natural quality-confirmation claim.

For each batch, all six permutations of full/native-eight/prefill execute under each of two sequential engines with maximum active sequences one and eight. A separately paid prefill call on the batch’s first row immediately precedes every permutation; this fixes the first arm’s predecessor while all permutations balance positions and within-order predecessors. Each engine receives its own three first-row warmups. Both explicitly use 32,768 batched tokens and chunked prefilling, BF16, eager execution, seed zero, and no prefix cache. This new robustness setting does not reproduce the earlier default scheduler or certify its exact speed percentage. Engine one precedes engine eight in one job, so cross-engine comparisons retain time/order confounding.

Complete clocks and accounting.

The complete plan contains 438 generate calls and 1,194 submitted sequences: 288 evidence-intervention sequences, 864 natural timing sequences, 36 conditioners, and six warmups. Each of the 108 actual eight-response timing calls has one whole-batch service clock beginning before fresh required input preparation and ending after generation, parsing, and the eight minimal alarm writes with flush/fsync calls. Dividing this clock by eight is amortized service, not individual latency. We report every engine/order/batch and descriptive ratio ranges. The three source batches with six repeated orders are not 108 independent natural samples or a production-tail estimate. Source qualification, both initializations, complete actual-ID diagnostics, conditioners, warmups, shutdown, failures, and allocation idle time remain paid; post-release CPU audit and scoring are separate. No warm-service ratio is assigned as an allocated-GPU, monetary, or energy saving.

Evidence-conditioned results.

All four readouts—full official-offset presence, full raw-list presence, Native8, and Prefill1—classify all 96 constructed inputs correctly. For each readout, all 24 quartets are completely correct and all 48 fixed-answer pairs receive the correct opposite decisions after the evidence change. Table 29 reports every prespecified domain. Each readout has 48 true positives, 48 true negatives, zero false positives, and zero false negatives; accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 are all 100%. Invalid-as-negative, invalid-as-positive, and strict-invalid-always-wrong summaries coincide because there are no invalid outputs. Full official and raw alarms reuse one generation, and all six pairwise readout comparisons agree on all 96 inputs.

This complete finite-pool result rules out a deterministic answer-only or context-only decision rule for these constructed records: without opaque identifiers, either feature alone permits at most 50% accuracy and no fully correct quartet. It supplies evidence that the shortened readouts retain the frozen detector’s literal evidence-conditioned behavior on this assay. The 96 crossed inputs form 24 deliberately constructed families, so the result is a complete-pool measurement of literal conditionality with family dependence retained in its interpretation.

Balanced-order runtime results.

Table 30 gives all three arms under each engine. Every arm has 18 actual eight-response timing calls per engine: three fixed source batches repeated under all six orders, totaling 144 submitted sequences. Whole-service totals include fresh preparation, generation, parsing, and minimal alarm writes. Prefill/full service ratios are 0.047143 and 0.074726 under maximum active sequences one and eight, respectively; prefill/native-eight ratios are 0.230934 and 0.618659. Thus the measured prefill reduction against full is 95.29% and 92.53%, while the reduction against native-eight is 76.91% and 38.13%. The latter benefit is smaller in the eight-active-sequence setting. These within-engine contrasts retain all orders rather than selecting the fastest ordering.

Table 31 reports all six orders for both engines. Each ratio there divides the summed services of the same three source batches. Separately, the ranges of the 18 paired batch ratios (three batches by six repeated orders) are as follows. With one active sequence, prefill/full ranges from 0.034517 to 0.055414, prefill/native-eight from 0.180695 to 0.312688, and native-eight/full from 0.177218 to 0.251142. With eight active sequences, the corresponding ranges are 0.030627–0.121499, 0.445771–0.788292, and 0.068707–0.164406. They describe these fixed repetitions; neither the ranges nor the 108 timed calls are independent-sample uncertainty intervals or production-tail estimates.

For every one of the 24 natural rows and each arm, the 12 observations across both engines and all orders have one unique generated token-ID sequence and one unique decision. This is an actual-output stability check, not a new natural quality measurement. All submitted outputs are valid. No full generation reaches its 1,024-token cap. Native-eight reaches its intentional eight-token limit on all 386 submitted sequences, and prefill-one reaches its intentional one-token limit on all 422, including intervention, timing, warmup, and conditioner phases as applicable. These planned short-output cap hits are retained rather than interpreted as full-output failures.

The engines run sequentially on one host in one allocation, with the one-active-sequence engine first. Consequently, a cross-engine change cannot be attributed solely to concurrency: elapsed time, cache state, and engine order remain confounded. Both engines explicitly use chunked prefilling and a 32,768 batched-token budget, which differs from the earlier scheduler defaults. The assay supports robustness of a useful within-generator operating point under this additional setting, not exact replication of the earlier percentage, production latency, quality equality, or fieldwide SOTA.

Complete execution, validation, and cost.

All 438 generate calls complete, covering 1,194 submitted sequences: 288 intervention, 864 natural timing, 36 conditioner, and six warmup sequences. Their respective complete service totals are 70.483, 250.602, 1.448, and 7.264 s. Total input/output tokens over all phases are 3,059,522/17,633. Engine initialization takes 150.423/39.677 s and shutdown 1.944/3.236 s for active-sequence limits one/eight; actual-ID diagnostics total 10.822 s. Asset verification and source tokenization preflight take 5.776 and 5.381 s. These component clocks are included in the 590.746 s worker wall time, not added to it as separate allocations. The main allocation is one GPU for 593 elapsed seconds, counted once, including setup, failures if any, and idle time. The independent post-job CPU ID auditor verifies all 1,194 sequences in 23.283 s internally; its collector process takes 24.897 s. A separate CPU-only pre-submission qualification takes 36.519 s without loading weights, constructing an engine, or generating outputs. Local scoring takes 0.333 CPU seconds, with no new model calls or GPU use. All audit checks pass and scoring reports zero issues. Warm-service ratios are not allocation, billing, monetary, or energy-saving estimates.

The initial local scorer refuses before reading references because its transport validator resolves fixed remote tokenizer/config paths to nonexistent Mac assets. A pinned validation-only revision instead uses the already collected independent remote CPU hash attestation for those exact assets; all other pins still require local bytes. The refusal and original scorer remain preserved. This changes no inference, method, source, route, metric, or output, and copies no model/tokenizer assets to the Mac. The completed score and aggregate tables refer to that strictly bounded transport repair.

Appendix F Matched-contract and optimized-execution controls

Two additional controls distinguish the usefulness of the native readout from that of its established inference primitives. The first preserves the verifier’s semantic instructions while replacing its output contract with a direct Boolean answer. The second tests whether moving syntax into prefill remains useful when the decoder uses its default compiled execution path. These controls reuse exposed development or label-blind timing inputs; they do not add an independent modern test cohort. All comparisons use the same frozen checkpoint and tokenizer revision as the focal readout.

F.1 A semantically matched binary contract

The complete Data2txt development source contains 1,026 responses in 171 six-response source components, with 715 positive and 311 negative references. The source was already exposed during development and originates from official TRAIN, so this comparison diagnoses a fixed interface choice rather than providing fresh confirmation. Every selected response is retained. References are evaluator-only and are not passed to either prompt construction or decoding.

The original opening definition of a hallucinated span, every category and subcategory definition, the evidence, answer, and user wrapper are byte-identical across arms. We replace the native action to quote and classify spans with the fixed instruction to determine whether any such span exists. The binary output contract requests a JSON object with has_annotated_error set to true or false. Its supplied prefix ends immediately after that key’s colon. We compare native Prefill1, unrestricted binary continuation, and masked binary continuation. Each generates one greedy token, with no prompt, threshold, or seed search. The mask is a stronger format control than unrestricted binary generation: it restricts the continuation to every legal single-token Boolean spelling, without changing the verification definition.

The legal alphabet is determined by syntax, not prediction quality. We enumerate all nonspecial vocabulary tokens, admit only ASCII JSON whitespace around true/false with an optional object-closing brace, and verify compositional decoding after the supplied prefix. The six accepted IDs are 804 (space–true), 867 (space–false), 1802 (true), 3721 (false), 34819 (tab–false), and 41393 (tab–true). No token in this vocabulary combines an admitted Boolean with the closing brace. The binary prefix IDs are (4754,4497,62,3292,639,3960,763)(4754,4497,62,3292,639,3960,763); the native seven IDs are unchanged. Both binary parsing and masking use the complete six-ID alphabet.

Table 32 reports the corrected comparison. Native Prefill1 has 677 true positives, 43 false positives, 38 false negatives, and 268 true negatives; masked binary has 630, 24, 85, and 287, respectively. The fixed-default native F1 difference is 2.32 points, with a paired 95% component-bootstrap interval of [1.10,3.59][1.10,3.59]. We resample the 171 whole source components with shared draws for both arms, using 2,000 replicates and seed 20261102. This interval conditions on the exposed cohort and the fixed outputs. It is not an independent-confirmation or equivalence interval. Among 70 disagreements, native is correct and binary wrong in 49 cases; the reverse occurs in 21. This default difference is a precision–recall tradeoff: masked binary has higher precision, while native retains more positive references. It is not dominance on every metric.

For unrestricted binary, 514 positive and 145 negative examples remain unknown. The remaining counts are 170 true positives, 11 false positives, 31 valid false negatives, and 155 true negatives. Strict all-item accuracy, counting every unknown as wrong, is 31.68%; the corresponding worst-case binary F1 bound is 32.66%. We neither repair these outputs nor discard them. However, format failures in this arm do not substitute for the fully valid masked comparison.

Each arm processes 33 batches of at most 32 responses, in original source order, with the three arm orders rotated by batch index. One singleton warmup per arm precedes the measurements. BF16 eager execution uses an active-sequence cap of eight, maximum context 16,384, no prefix caching, and greedy seed zero. There are 3,078 measured sequences plus three warmups. Fresh service includes fresh tokenization, synchronized generation, parsing, and per-alarm minimal synchronous writing. Native, masked binary, and free binary take 14.379, 14.661, and 14.481 seconds of measured service, respectively; their generation times are 10.068, 10.090, and 10.018 seconds. Native input/output totals are 1,471,501/1,026; both binary arms use 1,462,267/1,026. All supplied syntax is counted as input. These costs are comparable; the approximately 2% service difference is not the main efficiency result. Shared initialization takes 53.100 seconds, with qualification, warmup, and diagnostics separately retained.

This comparison describes one exposed-DEV operating point under a fixed, semantics-matched contract. We do not infer intrinsic quality superiority over calibrated binary readouts, or a causal need for span training. The exact prompts, engine settings, token alphabet, confusion counts, uncertainty specification, and phase costs accompany this appendix in the anonymous aggregate artifact.

F.2 Default compiled execution

The runtime control reuses 24 previously qualified label-blind inputs in three fixed batches of eight. Each batch is measured in both Native8–Prefill1 and Prefill1–Native8 order. We run four separate processes, in the fixed order eager with active-sequence cap one, optimized with cap one, optimized with cap eight, and eager with cap eight. Each process has 96 measured sequences and two singleton warmups, for 392 sequences in total. These are three fixed batches with repeated orders, not six independent samples or a new quality population.

All processes share BF16 arithmetic, maximum context and batched-token budgets of 32,768, chunked prefill enabled, prefix caching disabled, memory utilization 0.70, and seed zero. The requested intervention changes enforce_eager from true to false. The resulting default optimized execution uses the Inductor backend, compilation mode 3, and full-and-piecewise CUDA Graphs. The captured size sets are {1,2}\{1,2\} and {1,2,4,8,16}\{1,2,4,8,16\} for the two active-sequence caps. Raw process logs, in addition to configuration snapshots, confirm compilation and graph capture: the two optimized processes report 47.86 and 11.09 seconds for compilation and one and two seconds for capture. This comparison measures the default optimized path; it does not isolate the causal effect of CUDA Graphs from the compiler, backend, or cache state.

Table 33 shows a smaller but positive aggregate increment over native early stopping after optimization: Prefill1 reduces fresh service by 19.57% at cap one and 8.84% at cap eight. The corresponding median paired service ratios are .706 and .920; eager medians are .247 and .578. These summaries answer different questions: the ratio of totals weights batches by their Native8 duration, whereas the median gives each paired batch/order ratio equal weight. We report both rather than substituting the more favorable summary.

The benefit is not uniform across measurements (Table 34). Each arm has 48 measured sequences per process. Native8 input/output totals are 157,310/384 and Prefill1 totals are 157,646/48, giving the same 157,694 logical tokens. There are no invalid outputs or within-process branch disagreements. Across eager and optimized execution, all 192 matched output-ID and decision comparisons agree. This is observed agreement on the timing source, not a general finite-precision identity claim.

Initialization, including compilation or capture where applicable, takes 46.071, 88.540, 55.585, and 44.359 seconds in the stated process order. Warmups, source qualification, diagnostics, and initialization are charged to the complete allocation rather than selectively assigned to a favorable arm. The fresh-service clock includes tokenization, synchronized generation, parsing, and minimal alarm writing. It does not measure per-request response latency, concurrent-client serving, a complete application workflow, or proportional GPU billing. The smaller optimized increment also cautions against transferring an eager speedup unchanged to another runtime configuration.

F.3 Validity lineage and complete accounting

Two implementation defects were identified and retained rather than converted into apparent research gains. First, a CPU preflight assertion incorrectly expected the native seven-ID prefix to include the list opener. The prefix actually ends at the colon; the next generated token carries the list opener and branch. Only this assertion was corrected before GPU inference, with no change to the native prefix, prompt, or parser.

Second, the initial binary parser and mask admitted only bare true/false token IDs. A syntax audit found 366 legal leading-space Boolean outputs that the parser had rejected. That incomplete alphabet is not evidence of detection failure. We retained its raw outputs and superseded its capability comparison with the prospective, complete six-token grammar described above. The corrected three-arm run uses the same semantic prompts, inputs, and native readout; no label or performance ranking selects aliases. All corrected outputs, including the remaining 659 unrestricted-format failures, are retained. The paper’s matched-contract comparison uses only the corrected result.

The first allocation, containing the superseded binary comparison and all four runtime processes, consumes 577 GPU seconds; the corrected binary allocation consumes 167. Both are terminal, with one allocated GPU each. Their combined 744 GPU seconds include startup, qualification, diagnostics, failed-control work, and idle overhead. Complete project exploration therefore comprises 119 terminal allocations and 88,215 GPU seconds (24.5042 GPU hours), with zero pending reservation and zero paid API expenditure. These allocation costs are separate from service ratios and are not attributed to individual methods.

The separately maintained artifact archive contains interface_controls.csv for the reported aggregates and interface_controls.json for the exact contracts, token spellings, schedules, metrics, all paired runtime ratios, software versions, input/reference/code hashes, and complete cost scopes. Neither artifact contains individual inputs, identifiers, reference labels, or predictions. Raw instances and full execution evidence remain separately preserved; aggregate reconstruction and source hashes do not replace them for independent rerunning.

Appendix G Optimized execution on the complete workload

The full-workload control asks whether the extra saving over native early stopping survives both optimized execution and the complete set of 2,015 code-agent inputs. It extends the 24-input timing pilot; the checkpoint, native instruction, seven-token prefix, and alarm parser remain fixed. The primary comparison is the ratio of summed fresh-service times for Prefill1 and Native8. No labels, output-based selection, prompt search, or retries enter this timing measurement.

G.1 Workload and execution

The original input bytes are retained in their frozen order and partitioned into 63 chunks: 62 of size 32 and one of size 31. Each chunk is processed in both Native8–Prefill1 and Prefill1–Native8 order, with the initial order alternating by chunk index. Thus each arm processes every input twice: 4,030 measured sequences per arm at each active-sequence cap. Each process also has one singleton warmup per arm, giving 8,062 sequences including warmups. The two processes run sequentially on the same H100 80GB allocation, first with active-sequence cap S=1S=1, then S=8S=8. These are scheduler caps, not numbers of independent clients. The two order repetitions reuse the same inputs and are not independent quality samples.

Both processes use vLLM 0.17.1, BF16, greedy decoding with seed zero, context and batched-token limits of 32,768, chunked prefill enabled, memory utilization 0.70, and prefix caching disabled. There are no masks or log-probability requests in the timed calls. Default optimized execution uses Inductor compilation and full-and-piecewise CUDA Graphs. Process logs confirm loading compiled graphs and completing mixed prefill/decode and full-decode graph capture; this conclusion does not rely on configuration flags alone. Compilation caches are reused, so the experiment is not a cold-cache compilation benchmark. The graph capture sets are {1,2}\{1,2\} for S=1S=1 and {1,2,4,8,16}\{1,2,4,8,16\} for S=8S=8.

Every measured call freshly constructs and tokenizes its input, performs synchronized generation, parses the alarm, and minimally writes it with synchronous persistence. Their sum is the fresh-service clock. Qualification, initialization, warmup, and the more extensive actual-token-ID diagnostic serialization are timed separately. The first measured chunk remains in the reported totals. Each arm has exactly 17,242,482 measured logical tokens at each cap, across its two workload passes: Native8 uses 17,210,242 input and 32,240 output tokens; Prefill1 uses 17,238,452 input and 4,030 output tokens. The supplied syntax is therefore charged as input, rather than counted as free or deleted from the total.

G.2 Service savings and complete costs

Table 35 shows a positive aggregate increment over Native8 at both caps. The corresponding mean times for one complete workload pass are 125.060 versus 91.632 seconds at S=1S=1, and 83.154 versus 77.553 seconds at S=8S=8. The ratios of totals are .733 and .933; the medians of the 63 paired chunk totals are .733 and .934. Three of the 126 individual chunk/order measurements at S=8S=8 favor Native8. After summing both orders within each chunk, no chunk reverses at either cap. All of these observations are retained; a positive aggregate does not imply that every measured call is faster.

Generation alone takes 205.242 versus 138.392 seconds at S=1S=1 and 114.205 versus 102.709 seconds at S=8S=8, again summed over both passes. Model and engine initialization, including compilation/capture where applicable, takes 66.469 and 65.307 seconds for the two processes. The two warmups together take 2.186 and .956 seconds of service. Measured diagnostic serialization takes 124.202 and 133.989 seconds across both arms; source tokenization qualification takes 207.517 and 238.709 seconds. Complete worker wall times are 866.515 and 820.853 seconds. The single allocation consumes 1,697 GPU seconds, calculated from one allocated GPU times terminal main-job elapsed time, including all startup, checks, diagnostics, shutdown, and idle overhead. These costs are distinct from resident batch-service ratios. The experiment does not measure online single-request latency, concurrent-client throughput, end-to-end application savings, or proportional GPU billing.

G.3 Actual decisions and descriptive quality

All measured outputs are valid, but optimized execution is not strictly decision-invariant. Native8 and Prefill1 differ in 12 of 4,030 paired decisions at S=1S=1 and 13 of 4,030 at S=8S=8. At S=1S=1, both arms repeat identically. At S=8S=8, the two repetitions differ on six of 2,015 inputs for Native8 and one for Prefill1. Across scheduler caps, Native8 differs in 18 of 4,030 matched decisions and Prefill1 in nine; generated-ID differences have the same counts. These records preclude a claim of exact finite-precision trajectory equivalence.

After observing these differences, we recorded and performed a descriptive CPU-only join of the actual timed alarms to the already exposed, released code-agent references. No strategy or threshold was fitted, no new generation was run, and all four cap/repetition conditions were retained. Each condition contains the same 2,015 responses in 1,613 source components, with 1,014 positive and 1,001 negative references. This post hoc check attaches quality to the measured speed points; it is not a new independent quality confirmation.

For both S=1S=1 repetitions, Native8 precision/recall is 90.286/77.909 and Prefill1 is 90.263/77.712. At S=8S=8, repeat 0 gives 90.160/77.712 versus 90.400/78.008, and repeat 1 gives 90.183/77.909 versus 90.297/78.008. Prefill1 corrects versus introduces 2 versus 4 errors in each S=1S=1 repetition, 6 versus 1 at S=8S=8 repeat 0, and 4 versus 2 at repeat 1. The F1 changes in Table 36 are small but nonzero. Together with the full-workload service reduction, they support a useful, configuration-dependent quality–cost point, rather than lossless decoding or a general quality improvement. Complete aggregate phase costs, confusion counts, all 126 paired timing observations per cap, and artifact hashes are retained for audit.

Appendix H Artifact provenance and complete exploration costs

The preserved evidence manifest binds each completed scorer output to its SHA-256 digest, source/protocol identities, and actual allocation cost. It separates the prospective readout study from later exposed-cohort controls and replay. Original execution traces remain in the preserved experiment archives. The aggregate records retain failure costs, adverse outcomes, and correction lineage; they do not replace raw traces for independent rerunning.

The project ledger records 90,659 GPU-seconds (25.1831 GPU-hours) across 121 terminal allocations, including abandoned directions, loading, failures and idle/CPU work. This includes a 281-second qualification/timing pilot outside the labeled quality populations. The six-arm DEV assay, eleven-arm modern confirmation, earlier physical cascade and evidence/balanced-runtime assay contribute 479, 1,907, 999 and 593 seconds. The later binary/compiled controls and Boolean-grammar repair contribute 577 and 167 seconds; original and repaired results remain. The complete optimized workload adds 1,697 seconds; 747 seconds of auxiliary interface analysis outside this paper also remain counted. Each allocation is charged once. The complete ledger is preserved separately as exploration_costs.json. API expenditure is zero. Total exploration is distinct from method service and does not establish provider-price or energy savings.
